On the procedural axis, prophylaxis, when indicated by cardiac status, is directed at dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue or the periapical region of the teeth, or perforation of the oral mucosa. Routine, non-invasive interventions such as superficial restorations above the gingival margin, radiographs, the placement or adjustment of removable prosthodontic or orthodontic appliances, and the shedding of deciduous teeth are not considered to warrant prophylaxis. The unifying principle across all current frameworks, including NICE, is that meticulous oral health and regular dental care matter more than any single antibiotic dose. The bacteraemia data discussed in Section 3 require careful interpretation in this context. That invasive procedures produce more endocarditis-related bacteraemia than ordinary oral function is supported by randomised data: cumulative incidence across six blood draws was 23% after toothbrushing, 60% after extraction with placebo, and 33% after extraction with amoxicillin [ 10 ]. The per-event gradient is real; what Section 3 establishes is that lifetime cumulative exposure is nonetheless dominated by toothbrushing, because it recurs daily and extraction does not. The two findings are complementary. The gradient justifies treating extraction differently from toothbrushing, but no study grades IE risk, as opposed to bacteraemia, across the procedures on either side of the boundary the guidelines set; the classification is best read as a defensible operational convention rather than a validated risk boundary.

Periodontal Care and Lifelong Maintenance in the At-Risk Patient Periodontal treatment is a course of care extending over months and, in maintenance, over a lifetime; it therefore raises questions the guidelines answer only obliquely.

The first question is which periodontal procedures fall within the definition. The ESC and AHA trigger—manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region—captures subgingival scaling, root planing and periodontal surgery, and also, less obviously, periodontal probing and supragingival scaling, since both can provoke bleeding and measurable bacteraemia with IE-related organisms. Under ESC and AHA guidance, prophylaxis is normally recommended for these procedures in high-risk patients, as they were in the United Kingdom before 2008. The empirical picture is more complex than the classification implies: in a cohort study of nearly eight million individuals, the association with IE in high-risk patients was concentrated in extractions (OR 9.22; 95% CI 5.54–15.88) and oral surgery (OR 20.18; 95% CI 11.22–36.74), whereas scaling was associated with a lower incidence of IE (OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.26–0.81), most plausibly because patients who attend for regular scaling have better oral health. The parallel case-crossover analysis, in which each patient serves as their own control and time-invariant characteristics such as oral hygiene are thereby held constant, showed the same pattern (extractions OR 11.08, 95% CI 7.34–16.74; oral surgery OR 50.77, 95% CI 20.79–123.98; scaling OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.47–1.02, not significant) [ 12 ]. This reflects the healthy-adherer effect discussed in Section 7 and illustrates why the invasive/non-invasive dichotomy, although operationally useful, does not correspond precisely to risk.

The second concerns repeated exposure. Quadrant-by-quadrant debridement may span several appointments within weeks, and maintenance implies recall every three to four months indefinitely; covering every visit would convert a single-dose intervention into recurrent antibiotic exposure over decades—a pattern that antimicrobial stewardship principles ( Section 8 ) seek to avoid. Where repeated prophylaxis is unavoidable, the AHA suggests an interval of 10 days between procedures requiring prophylaxis [ 4 ]; consolidating treatment into fewer, longer visits further reduces both cumulative exposure and selection pressure.

The third, and the most consequential in practice, concerns sequencing. Periodontal inflammation should not be regarded merely as an indication for prophylaxis before treatment; it is itself the dominant source of the everyday bacteraemia described in Section 3 , and the rationale for treating it is therefore stronger than that for providing antibiotic cover during treatment. The logic of the bacteraemia argument implies that a high-risk patient with untreated periodontitis is exposed to more oral streptococcal seeding between appointments than the appointments themselves contribute, and that leaving disease untreated out of caution about prophylaxis reverses the balance of risk. Where a patient is awaiting valve surgery, this becomes a matter of timing: dental assessment and the elimination of active infection ideally precede elective implantation, since the postoperative period is when the consequences of an oral-origin bacteraemia are gravest.

5. The Evolution of Prophylaxis Guidelines Understanding the present disagreement requires a brief historical orientation. The following overview is deliberately selective and focuses on the aspects that explain the present divergence: the progressive narrowing of the indication and the differing responses of each body to the same absence of trial evidence. For much of the late twentieth century, expansive antibiotic prophylaxis was recommended for a wide range of cardiac conditions before numerous dental and non-dental procedures, on a largely empirical and precautionary basis. The early twenty-first century brought a decisive reappraisal, driven by three converging concerns: the absence of randomised evidence demonstrating that prophylaxis actually prevents IE; mounting awareness of the harms of antibiotics, including anaphylaxis and the societal cost of antimicrobial resistance; and the recognition, discussed above, that cumulative everyday bacteraemia overshadows procedure-related exposure [ 13 ].

In 2007, the AHA substantially narrowed its recommendations, restricting prophylaxis to the highest-risk cardiac categories and abandoning prophylaxis based on lifetime acquisition risk alone; the American Dental Association endorsed this approach as it related to dentistry [ 14 , 15 ]. The 2021 AHA scientific statement reviewed the intervening evidence and recommended no substantive change, reaffirming the restricted high-risk approach while emphasising oral health; it also removed clindamycin from the recommended regimens because of its disproportionate risk of adverse effects, including Clostridioides difficile infection [ 4 ]. The 2023 ESC guidelines, having reviewed the accumulated evidence, retained the high-risk focus but m moved in the opposite direction to NICE, strengthening the recommendation for prophylaxis in high-risk patients to Class I and allowing that it may be considered on an individual basis in moderate-risk patients (Class IIb) [ 3 ].

NICE reached the opposite conclusion from the same evidence base because it applied a higher evidentiary threshold and treated the intervention, rather than its omission, as the option requiring positive justification. Its 2008 guideline concluded that the evidence did not justify routine prophylaxis and advised against it for all patients, a position more categorical than that adopted by other bodies, and one that follows from its stated requirement for demonstrated efficacy rather than from any disagreement about the underlying data [ 5 ]. A 2016 amendment softened the wording, inserting the word “routinely” so that the guidance read that prophylaxis is not recommended routinely, but it did not restore a positive recommendation [ 6 ]. This amendment followed NICE’s 2015 review of the evidence [ 5 ] and was a change in wording rather than of substance; the underlying recommendation has not been materially revised since. In October 2024, NICE undertook an exceptional surveillance review of the evidence, including the contemporary meta-analytic data; it concluded that robust evidence remained lacking and left the substance of the CG64 recommendation unchanged. The same review now signposts the implementation advice of the Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme (SDCEP), which helps identify the subset of higher-risk patients warranting special consideration for prophylaxis [ 16 ]. The core NICE position (no positive recommendation for routine prophylaxis) has thus remained essentially unchanged, even as its practical framing has been nuanced. This trajectory left United Kingdom guidance increasingly divergent from international practice as the ESC and AHA reaffirmed and, in the ESC’s case, strengthened a role for prophylaxis in the highest-risk group.

6. The Central Divergence: ESC/AHA Versus NICE The core of the current controversy may be summarised as follows. The ESC and AHA, while differing in emphasis and in a few specific criteria, agree that a defined group of highest-risk cardiac patients should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures. NICE, alone among major bodies, advises against routine prophylaxis for any group. A dental patient with a prosthetic heart valve facing an extraction would, therefore, in much of Europe and North America, be offered prophylaxis as a matter of course, yet, under a literal reading of NICE guidance in England and Wales, might receive none. This discordance is a source of uncertainty in clinical practice.

It is important to characterise the ESC and AHA as broadly concordant rather than identical. Both restrict prophylaxis to the highest-risk categories and both prioritise oral health. The differences are at the margins: the ESC explicitly contemplates individualised prophylaxis in moderate-risk patients (Class IIb), an option not included in the AHA statement; the AHA places cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy in the highest-risk group, whereas the ESC treats heart transplant recipients as a Class IIb consideration—a move towards the AHA, since the 2015 ESC guidelines had explicitly declined to recommend prophylaxis for this group [ 13 ]; and the two differ in minor respects regarding certain repaired congenital lesions and conduits. For the dental practitioner, these distinctions rarely change management of the clearly highest-risk patient, but they matter at the boundaries and they illustrate that even “aligned” guidelines are not interchangeable.

The NICE position should be understood on its own terms rather than dismissed as incorrect. It rests on a defensible reading that the efficacy of prophylaxis has never been demonstrated in a randomised trial, that the number of cases potentially preventable is very small even under optimistic assumptions, and that the harms and costs of widespread antibiotic use are real. Its critics counter that absence of randomised evidence is not evidence of absence of effect, that the consequences of an IE case are catastrophic and the harm of a single prophylactic dose minimal, and that observational data have since shifted in favour of a protective effect [ 17 , 18 ]. The NICE position may be summarised in its strongest form as follows. Even if the pooled relative risk of approximately 0.41 [ 18 ] is taken at face value, prophylaxis before invasive dental procedures could avert only a small minority of IE cases in high-risk patients, since such procedures account for only a fraction of cases; the number needed to treat is correspondingly very large, because the absolute risk after any single procedure is very low, even in a high-risk patient. Against that, every dose contributes to selection pressure at population level. The disagreement is therefore not a simple matter of one body being right and another wrong; it is a genuine difference in how the same imperfect evidence is weighed against the same competing harms. All three bodies accept that no randomised evidence exists, that the observational signal is real but confounded, and that the number of preventable cases is small; what separates them is the evidentiary threshold each applies before recommending an intervention. That threshold is not itself derivable from the data, which is why the contradiction cannot be settled by another observational study.

Across most of continental Europe, this divergence does not arise in the same way, because the ESC guidelines function as the operative standard and are disseminated through national cardiological societies, which typically translate and endorse them rather than issue competing advice [ 3 ]. The practical implication is that a dentist working anywhere within the ESC-aligned European setting will generally follow the same risk-stratified approach centred on the highest-risk group, and the disagreement described above is therefore felt most acutely in the United Kingdom rather than across Europe as a whole.

7. The Contested Epidemiological Evidence Because no randomised controlled trial has ever tested whether antibiotic prophylaxis prevents IE, and because the rarity of the disease makes such a trial very difficult to power adequately—while withholding prophylaxis from an identified highest-risk patient raises an ethical objection that individual randomisation cannot easily answer—the debate has so far relied on observational and population-level evidence. This evidence is inconsistent, and a balanced appraisal requires consideration of studies on both sides.

The most influential study supporting a protective role examined IE incidence in England before and after the 2008 NICE guidance [ 17 ]. It reported that prescriptions of prophylaxis fell substantially after the guideline, and that the incidence of IE rose significantly above the projected historical trend, with a meaningful number of additional cases per month by the end of the study period; notably, the increase was observed across both higher-risk and lower-risk groups. The authors were careful to state that their interrupted time-series design could not establish causation, only temporal association, and that other secular trends in the epidemiology of IE could contribute. Nonetheless, the temporal coincidence of falling prophylaxis and rising incidence has been widely cited as evidence that withdrawing prophylaxis may have caused harm. This inference is not supported by the study design. The study’s own finding that incidence rose in both higher-risk and lower-risk groups is hard to reconcile with a causal effect of withdrawing prophylaxis, since prophylaxis was never indicated in the lower-risk group. A more parsimonious interpretation is that a common cause—an ageing population, more prosthetic and transcatheter implantation, rising injection drug use, improved ascertainment and coding—drove incidence upward in both groups, and that the guideline change is confounded with calendar time. An interrupted time-series can identify an effect only if the counterfactual trend is correctly specified; here, the pre-intervention trend was itself rising, and the estimate is sensitive to the functional form chosen for extrapolation. This is ecological inference: an association between two population-level time series cannot license a claim about individual-level causation.

Other studies have not consistently supported this finding. An earlier before-and-after analysis, by an overlapping group of investigators, had found no statistically significant increase in IE cases following the same guideline, although it was able to exclude only increases above a certain threshold [ 19 ]. Studies from other settings have likewise been inconsistent: a Swedish national cohort study in high-risk individuals could not confirm that invasive dental procedures were more frequent before IE than expected, including during the period when Swedish dentistry had ceased prophylaxis [ 20 ]. The discrepancies reflect the inherent limitations of population-level and observational study designs: confounding by secular trends, changes in coding and case ascertainment, shifts in the microbial epidemiology of IE, and the difficulty of attributing a rare outcome to a specific exposure [ 21 ]. Appraised against the ROBINS-I domains [ 7 ], no study in this literature reaches low risk of bias overall, and none is likely to while randomisation is unavailable; confounding is judged serious throughout, and classification of exposure is a further serious concern in the prescription-based studies, where dispensing records serve as a proxy for actual intake and timing. Two mechanisms make this confounding difficult to address in data of this kind. Confounding by indication operates in both directions: clinicians prescribe preferentially to patients they judge highest risk, which biases towards the null, while those who receive prophylaxis are also under active cardiological follow-up, which biases away from it. And patients who attend for prophylaxis are, by construction, patients engaged with dental care—itself protective through better oral health, a pathway no published adjustment separates from the effect of the antibiotic.

One defensible reading of the contemporary observational evidence is that it has, on balance, moved in the direction of supporting a protective effect of prophylaxis in genuinely high-risk patients, and this is the shift the ESC cited in strengthening its recommendation; a reader who sets a higher evidentiary threshold, or who weights the population-level costs of antibiotic exposure more heavily, can read the same body of work as not yet warranting a change in practice [ 18 , 22 ]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis, for example, found that prophylaxis was associated with a significantly lower risk of IE following invasive dental procedures in high-risk individuals (pooled relative risk approximately 0.41, 95% confidence interval 0.29 to 0.57) [ 18 ]; the same review found no association in those at low or unknown risk and judged the available data insufficient to support any benefit at moderate risk, which bears directly on the ESC’s Class IIb allowance for that group. Invasive dental procedures are thought to account for only a minority of IE cases, even in high-risk patients. But this evidence remains associative, susceptible to confounding, and incapable of proving causation [ 23 ]. The case for causation is partial: biological plausibility, temporality and a coherent mechanism are satisfied, but the association is of moderate strength, no dose–response relationship has been shown, and no experimental evidence exists. Consistency depends on which studies are admitted—heterogeneity within the 2024 meta-analysis was absent (I 2 = 0%) [ 18 ], yet the studies outside its pooled estimate did not detect the effect. The confounding described above is not, however, unlimited in what it can explain: a confounder would have to be strongly associated with both prophylaxis receipt and IE to account for an effect of this size, and whether the healthy-adherer and indication effects reach that magnitude is unresolved. The constraint is symmetrical, since the null findings cannot exclude a modest benefit either. The most that can be claimed is that the data are compatible with a modest protective effect in the highest-risk group; they do not establish it, and they do not support a return to the expansive prophylaxis of earlier decades. It follows that the ESC’s elevation of prophylaxis to a Class I recommendation—a class reserved for interventions for which there is evidence and/or general agreement that a treatment is beneficial and effective—rests on general agreement rather than on evidence of the strength that designation ordinarily connotes. That is a legitimate use of the class system, which explicitly permits consensus to substitute for data, but it is easily misread by clinicians as an evidentiary claim, and this review does not endorse it as one.

8. Recommended Regimens and Responsible Antibiotic Use Where prophylaxis is indicated, the recommended approach across the ESC and AHA frameworks is a single oral dose given shortly before the procedure, timed to achieve adequate serum concentrations during the period of anticipated bacteraemia; if inadvertently omitted, the dose may be given up to 2 h after the procedure, according to the AHA [ 4 ]. The standard agent in the absence of penicillin allergy is amoxicillin, with ampicillin, cefazolin, or ceftriaxone as parenteral alternatives when oral administration is not feasible. For patients with penicillin or ampicillin allergy, a cephalosporin (in the absence of a history of severe allergy to penicillins) or another suitable agent such as a macrolide or doxycycline is selected according to the specific guideline [ 3 , 4 ]; representative regimens are shown in Table 2 . Two aspects of these recommendations merit comment. First, the regimen structure—single dose, timed to the procedure, aimed at the window of bacteraemia—is supported only by observational studies and animal models rather than by clinical outcome data [ 13 ]. No trial has tested the schedule against any alternative; the 2 g dose and 30–60 min window are validated against measured bacteraemia [ 10 ], not IE incidence. Second, the guidelines are more confident about the agent than the indication: the same documents that hedge the decision to prescribe specify drug and dose without qualification. This asymmetry is understandable, as pharmacokinetic questions are more readily investigated than epidemiological ones, but it may lead readers to infer that the underlying question is more settled than it is.

A noteworthy development in responsible antibiotic use is the removal of clindamycin from the recommended regimens by both the AHA and contemporary European guidance. Clindamycin was previously a standard alternative for penicillin-allergic patients, but it carries a disproportionate risk of adverse effects, particularly Clostridioides difficile colitis, relative to other options [ 4 ]. Its removal exemplifies the broader principle now embedded in the guidelines: that the harms of the antibiotic itself, both to the individual and to the wider problem of antimicrobial resistance, are weighed explicitly against the small and uncertain preventive benefit. A further practical point is that a patient already taking an antibiotic of the penicillin class for another reason should be given a prophylactic agent from a different class.

Dentists are among the highest-volume prescribers of antibiotics in ambulatory care, and much of what they prescribe as prophylaxis is unsupported by any guideline discussed here. In a US cohort of 91,438 patients covering 168,420 dental visits (2011–2015), gingival or periapical manipulation occurred at 90.7% of visits but only 20.9% of patients had a highest-risk cardiac condition; 80.9% of prophylaxis prescriptions were discordant with guidelines. Unnecessary prophylaxis was associated with prosthetic joint devices (OR 2.31; 95% CI 2.22–2.41) and implant procedures (OR 1.66; 95% CI 1.45–1.89), and was more likely when clindamycin rather than amoxicillin was prescribed (OR 1.10; 95% CI 1.05–1.15) [ 24 ]. The practical stewardship problem is therefore not the small number of correctly indicated doses but the much larger volume of prescribing that no guideline supports.

Evidence on individual harm has also become clearer. Across nearly three million prescriptions of single-dose amoxicillin prophylaxis in England, then given as 3 g, no fatal reaction was recorded, against 13 per million for clindamycin, most of them Clostridioides difficile infections [ 25 , 26 ]. The objection that a single prophylactic dose is unsafe for the individual patient is therefore not supported by these figures, and the withdrawal of clindamycin from the recommended regimens removed most of the risk on which that objection rested; the argument for restraint now rests on antimicrobial resistance rather than on individual harm. In practical terms, the greatest potential gain lies not in moving the prophylaxis threshold in either direction but in eliminating the prescribing that lies outside every guideline, and in recording each prophylaxis decision—indication, cardiac condition, procedure, agent and dose—so that it can be audited.

9. The Perspective of Dental Organisations National dental bodies have, for the most part, not issued prophylaxis criteria of their own but have adopted or operationalised the cardiological guidance for the dental setting, and their statements are therefore instructive as to how the debate is translated into clinical practice. In the United States, the American Dental Association (ADA) aligns with the AHA position, advising that prophylaxis be reserved for the small subset of patients at the highest risk of an adverse outcome and that, for many patients formerly considered eligible, the risk of antibiotic adverse effects and the concern over resistance outweigh any benefit [ 15 ]. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry takes a similarly restrictive view, noting explicitly that the evidence for efficacy in children is limited and that prudence is required given the risks of resistance and adverse events [ 27 ]. The Canadian Dental Association likewise endorses the AHA approach, emphasising that most patients with a cardiac history do not require routine prophylaxis and that good oral health and regular dental access are the more important protective measures [ 28 ].

The most consequential dental contribution, however, has come from the United Kingdom, where the ambiguity of the NICE guidance left dentists without a workable definition of the “non-routine” situations in which prophylaxis might still be appropriate. To fill that gap, the Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme (SDCEP) produced implementation advice, first issued in 2018 and substantially revised in a second edition in 2026, that supports dental teams in applying CG64 [ 29 ]. Its key messages are that prophylaxis is recommended or should be considered for patients with high-risk cardiac conditions, is not recommended for those at moderate risk, and that the decision for an at-risk dental procedure should be made jointly with the patient; it also identifies a specific sub-group of higher-risk patients warranting special consideration for non-routine management. Notably, the SDCEP advice aligns with the AHA and ESC on which patients should be considered for prophylaxis, even though it differs in the specific antibiotic regimens it recommends. Its practical importance was formally recognised in October 2024, when NICE amended CG64 to signpost the SDCEP advice directly, and again in December 2024, when the same recommendation and its reference to that advice were further clarified, thereby narrowing, without closing, the gap between the literal NICE position and that of the ESC and AHA [ 16 ]. The common thread across all these bodies is unanimity on the primacy of oral health and shared, documented decision-making, with the residual disagreement concerning only the narrow question of whether and when to prescribe.

Oral Health as the Cornerstone of Prevention One of the few points of genuine unanimity across the ESC, AHA, and NICE is that the maintenance of good oral health is more important to the prevention of oral-origin IE than any antibiotic dose before a procedure. This consensus follows directly from the bacteraemia argument: if the great majority of oral streptococcal seeding of the bloodstream arises from the cumulative effect of daily activities in the presence of dental plaque and gingival inflammation, then reducing this bacterial and inflammatory load addresses the dominant source of exposure, whereas a single prophylactic dose addresses only the small procedural fraction [ 10 ].

For the dental team, this reframes the preventive task. Rather than viewing IE prevention as a question answered solely at the moment of prescribing, the dentist’s most consequential contribution is the establishment and maintenance of periodontal and dental health in at-risk patients: effective plaque control, treatment of gingivitis and periodontitis, prompt management of dental infection, and regular review. Poor oral hygiene has itself been identified as a risk factor for IE-related bacteraemia [ 30 ]. The corollary is that high-risk cardiac patients warrant proactive, structured dental care and education, and that access to such care is a public-health priority in its own right, independent of the prophylaxis debate.

10. Limitations Several limitations should be borne in mind. This is a narrative rather than a systematic review, and is therefore subject to selection bias in the choice and emphasis of sources; methodological appraisal was narrative rather than score-based, and no quantitative synthesis was undertaken. Screening and selection were performed by a single author without duplicate assessment, so selective emphasis cannot be excluded and the review does not claim the reproducibility of a systematic review. The appraisal in Section 7 is narrative: it reasons about the plausibility of unmeasured confounding rather than constituting formal quantitative bias analysis. The author has no involvement with any guideline body and declares no relevant interest, but reviews of contested topics reflect the author’s prior weighting of harms; the position adopted here—that neither the ESC nor the NICE stance is established by the evidence, and that what separates them is the evidentiary threshold each body applies rather than the data themselves—represents the author’s interpretation. The underlying evidence base is itself a fundamental limitation: the central questions (whether prophylaxis prevents IE, and in whom) have not been answered by randomised controlled trials, leaving the field reliant for the present on observational and population-level data that cannot establish causation and that are vulnerable to confounding and to changes in the epidemiology of the disease. Guidelines also evolve, and specific criteria, regimens, and wording cited here may be superseded; readers must consult the current primary documents applicable to their jurisdiction. Finally, the review centres on oral-origin, viridans-streptococcal disease amenable to dental prophylaxis and does not address in depth the prevention of healthcare-associated, staphylococcal, or device-related IE, which lies largely outside the dental remit.

11. Future Directions The most valuable advances would come from study designs capable of reducing the present uncertainty without requiring an individually randomised trial, which remains impracticable. Large, linked, prospective cohort and registry studies, connecting dental, prescription, and hospital records across whole populations, offer the most realistic route to quantifying the effect of prophylaxis in genuinely high-risk patients while adjusting for confounders. Harmonisation of the international guidelines, or at least an explicit reconciliation of the ESC/AHA and NICE positions accompanied by a shared appraisal of the same evidence, would reduce the discordance that currently affects clinicians and patients. Research into the relationship between specific measures of oral health and IE incidence could strengthen the evidential basis for the prevention strategy on which all bodies already agree. Finally, work on better risk stratification, identifying which high-risk patients derive the greatest benefit, would allow prophylaxis to be targeted more precisely, maximising benefit while minimising antibiotic exposure.

12. Conclusions The prevention of oral-origin infective endocarditis sits at an unusual and unresolved intersection of cardiology and dentistry. The contemporary guidelines agree on more than is sometimes appreciated: that prophylaxis, if used, belongs to the highest-risk patient; that, where a regimen is specified, the antibiotic of choice is amoxicillin and that clindamycin should no longer be used; and, above all, that the maintenance of good oral health outweighs any pre-procedural dose. Yet, on the central question of whether to offer prophylaxis at all, the strengthened Class I endorsement of the ESC and the closely aligned position of the AHA remain at odds with the long-standing NICE advice against routine use, and that discordance is real and consequential, and cannot currently be resolved on the basis of definitive evidence. This review’s argument is that the discordance reflects the limitations of the available evidence rather than an error by either body: on the evidence as it stands, the ESC’s Class I recommendation is better read as an expression of expert consensus than as a demonstrated effect, while the NICE position remains a defensible reading of the same data. Recognising this is of greater value to the clinician than attempting to determine which position is correct, because it identifies the part of the decision that the evidence can settle—which is smaller than commonly supposed—and the part that must be settled with the patient. For the dental practitioner, the constructive response is neither to disregard the issue nor to defer decisions pending a resolution that may not be forthcoming: it is to know which framework governs one’s practice, to apply it consistently, to place oral health at the centre of prevention, and to make and document decisions jointly with well-informed patients. Until stronger evidence emerges, careful, transparent, individualised practice is the most appropriate standard of care.

Background : Despite continuous advancements in diagnostic imaging and targeted antimicrobial protocols for infective endocarditis (IE), global epidemiological data show that both disease burden and incidence continue to rise. This study aimed to evaluate real-world diagnostic and treatment approaches in accordance with the 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) IE Guidelines and to identify independent predictors of mortality in a contemporary patient cohort. Methods : This multicenter, retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 470 consecutive adult patients diagnosed with IE across 27 academic reference centers between 1 September 2023 and 1 June 2025. Patients were managed and adjudicated according to the 2023 ESC diagnostic criteria. Demographic data, clinical characteristics, microbiological profiles, imaging findings, empirical antibiotic therapy patterns, and clinical outcomes were analyzed. Independent predictors of mortality were determined using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models. Results : The mean age of the overall study population was 58.08 ± 16.81 years, with a male predominance (60.6%, n = 285). Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently isolated pathogen (27.9%), with a high proportion of methicillin resistance (38.9%). Hospital-acquired IE was identified in 41.1% of cases. Surgical treatment was performed in 40.6% ( n = 191) of the cohort. The 28-day mortality rate was 11.9%, and the overall mortality during follow-up reached 26.4%. Multivariable Cox regression analysis identified hospital-acquired IE (HR = 2.247; 95% CI: 1.216–4.167; p = 0.010) and the presence of major clinical complications (HR = 4.207; 95% CI: 1.556–11.378; p = 0.005) as the strongest independent predictors of mortality. Conclusions : Contemporary infective endocarditis is a highly complex and fatal disease characterized by a prominent healthcare-associated burden and a predominant staphylococcal etiology. Introduction Infective endocarditis (IE), situated at the intersection of cardiovascular medicine, infectious diseases, and clinical microbiology, remains a critical clinical condition characterized by varying clinical profiles, an altered microbiological spectrum, and persistently high mortality rates [ 1 , 2 ]. Despite continuous advancements in diagnostic imaging and targeted antimicrobial protocols, global epidemiological data show that both disease burden and incidence continue to rise [ 2 , 3 ]. Over the past few decades, the predisposing factors for IE have undergone a significant transformation; while the proportion of classical substrates such as rheumatic valvular disease has declined, there has been a marked increase in infections associated with degenerative valvular disease, prosthetic valve replacement, and cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) [ 1 , 4 ].

IE occurs with a higher incidence in males, elderly individuals, and patients with chronic kidney disease (particularly those undergoing hemodialysis), as well as in those who have undergone solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, an intravascular catheter, or predisposing cardiac conditions compared to the general population. Cardiac conditions predisposing to IE include the presence of intracardiac foreign bodies such as prosthetic valves, cardiac implantable electronic devices, or ventricular assist devices, as well as a history of prior IE, structural valvular heart diseases, and congenital heart diseases [ 1 , 5 , 6 ]. Streptococci or staphylococci are the causative agents in 80% of IE cases. In recent years, as a result of the increase in healthcare-associated IE cases, S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci have become more frequent pathogens, whereas the proportion of viridans group streptococci has relatively decreased [ 6 , 7 , 8 ].

Improving clinical outcomes in IE requires rapid diagnostic strategies and a structured multidisciplinary approach [ 5 ]. Identifying the causative microorganism in IE is critical for diagnosis and guiding antimicrobial treatment. Mortality increases when the causative agent of IE cannot be identified [ 1 , 4 , 5 ]. While transthoracic (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remain the primary diagnostic methods, cardiac computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and nuclear imaging techniques are also used to evaluate paravalvular complications, prosthetic valve dysfunction, and embolic foci. Effective antimicrobial treatment in IE is crucial for survival. Timely and appropriate selection of antibiotics in the management of IE reduces the development of severe sepsis, multiple organ failure, the risk of embolism, morbidity, and mortality [ 7 ].

The 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines introduced significant innovations regarding the updating of diagnostic criteria, the integration of novel imaging modalities into the system, and the clarification of early surgical indications in high-embolic-risk cases [ 1 ]. However, more data are needed on adopting these guideline recommendations in real-world clinical practice. In recent years, healthcare-associated infective endocarditis has emerged as a particularly vulnerable and high-risk clinical phenotype, driven by the increasing burden of invasive medical procedures, chronic hemodialysis, and frequent healthcare encounters. Unlike traditional community-acquired cases, healthcare-associated endocarditis is frequently associated with resistant pathogens, delays in diagnosis and treatment, and a much heavier burden of comorbidities; all of these factors contribute to an unacceptably high mortality rate. Despite its growing epidemiological importance, real-world data regarding the distinct prognostic impact and clinical course of healthcare-associated endocarditis remain limited [ 8 , 9 ]. In particular, the impact of current microbiological shifts on clinical outcomes and the independent predictors of survival in complex patient cohorts remain relevant research topics [ 4 , 6 ].

This study aims to evaluate real-world diagnostic and treatment approaches following the current ESC IE guideline. Subsequent aims are to examine the demographic characteristics, underlying microbiological agents, and anatomical complications of IE patients, as well as to identify independent clinical, echocardiographic, and biochemical parameters associated with mortality. Specifically, to address the gaps in real-world clinical practice, this multicenter study focuses on three primary objectives: (1) evaluating whether clinical centers adhere to the 2023 ESC recommendations for empirical antibiotic therapy in light of the changing spectrum of responsible bacteria and determining the impact of appropriateness on prognosis; (2) assessing the precise prognostic impact and clinical implications of hospital-acquired infective endocarditis; and (3) refining the independent in-hospital determinants and predictors of survival in a contemporary nationwide cohort of definite endocarditis patients following this guideline.

2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design and Setting This multicenter, retrospective cohort study was conducted across 27 academic reference centers, utilizing pooled data from specialized clinical divisions of cardiology, infectious diseases, and clinical microbiology. Patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and laboratory variables were systematically extracted from integrated electronic medical archives and registry databases for consecutive adult patients managed between 1 September 2023 and 1 June 2025. The study protocol was conducted in strict compliance with the ethical commitments of the Declaration of Helsinki. Administrative approval for data collection and analysis was granted by the Medical Ethics Committee of the coordinating academic institution.

2.2. Patient Selection and Diagnostic Definitions All adult individuals (>18 years) admitted to the participating hospital with a diagnosis of IE during the observation period were screened for eligibility. To ensure methodological consistency and eliminate diagnostic bias across the study timeline, all historical and active cases were systematically re-evaluated and adjudicated based on the 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines Diagnostic Criteria [ 1 ]. Only patients fulfilling the criteria for “Definite IE” as defined by the updated guidelines were included in the statistical analysis. To prevent statistical confounding linked to recurrent infectious episodes, only the index presentation of IE for each patient was considered.

The exclusion criteria were defined as Patient age under 18 years; A history of out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation or a state of refractory cardiogenic shock at the time of initial emergency department evaluation; Missing or substantially incomplete clinical, microbiological, or echocardiographic documentation within the registries.

2.3. Clinical, Microbiological, and Echocardiographic Evaluation Baseline clinical profiles, including age, gender, detailed comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and prior endocardial infections), and predisposing structural substrates (prosthetic heart valves, central venous catheters, or indwelling CIEDs) were thoroughly documented. Individual cases were classified by mode of acquisition into community-acquired IE or hospital-acquired IE. Specifically, hospital-acquired IE comprised infections developing at least 48 h after hospital admission or those diagnosed within 48 h in patients with significant recent healthcare exposures (such as maintenance hemodialysis, recent hospitalization, or chronic central venous catheterization), thereby ensuring that these clinical risk factors were appropriately accounted for within the acquisition classification.

Microbiological evaluation involved analyzing data from consecutive peripheral blood cultures, serological assays, and intraoperative valve tissue cultures or targeted molecular assays where available. Microbiological response was defined as the documentation of blood culture negativization evaluated on the 7th day of appropriate antimicrobial therapy in culture-positive patients. Complete echocardiographic examinations (comprising transthoracic and subsequent transesophageal evaluations as clinically indicated) performed by certified imaging specialists were comprehensively reviewed. Advanced anatomical destruction parameters were systematically recorded during the index hospitalization, specifically focusing on

Maximum vegetation length (stratified at standard clinical cut-offs of >10 mm, and critical measurements > 15 mm); Development of perivalvular abscesses or pseudoaneurysms; New-onset or progressive paravalvular leakage (PVL); Valve leaflet disruption or perforation.

2.4. Protocol for Empirical Antimicrobial Therapy Data regarding the administration of initial empirical antimicrobial regimens were systematically evaluated to assess adherence to contemporary international standards. Medical records were reviewed to verify whether a standardized protocol requiring three consecutive sets of blood cultures obtained at thirty-minute intervals had been consistently followed prior to initiating antimicrobial agents. The selection of initial empirical therapy was individualized based on several key clinical determinants:

Prior Treatment Status: Adjustments were applied for individuals with a recent history of antimicrobial therapy to ensure adequate and non-overlapping spectrum. Infection Substrate and Valve Status: Therapeutic strategies for native valve infections and late prosthetic valve involvement were structured to target staphylococcal, streptococcal, and enterococcal pathogens, with coagulase-negative staphylococci specifically incorporated into prosthetic valve protocols. Conversely, early prosthetic or healthcare-associated episodes required an expanded antimicrobial spectrum encompassing methicillin-resistant staphylococci, enterococci, and non-HACEK Gram-negative bacteria.

Epidemiological Context and Acquisition Origin: Stratification between community-onset and healthcare-associated acquisition was evaluated alongside institutional resistance profiles. Microbiological Customization: Following initial administration, regimens were swiftly adjusted to pathogen-directed targeted therapy once definitive susceptibility reports became available, typically within a 24-to-48-h window.

Appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy was defined as the initiation of an antimicrobial regimen fully concordant with current international guidelines, taking into account native versus prosthetic valve status, healthcare-associated versus community-acquired acquisition, and institutional epidemiological resistance patterns, and subsequently optimized according to blood culture isolation and susceptibility results. 2.5. Endpoint Assessment and Clinical Stratification The study cohort was stratified into two distinct clinical groups based on the primary clinical outcome documented during the follow-up period: Group 1 (Mortality): Patients who died during the follow-up period.
Group 2 (Survivors): Patients who completed their prescribed medical and/or surgical therapy and were alive at the end of available follow-up.

Secondary clinical complications monitored across the retrospective observation window included the incidence of acute congestive heart failure, systemic or peripheral embolic events (including central nervous system embolic stroke, visceral splenic infarction, and acute pulmonary embolism), persistent uncontrolled bacteremia, new-onset cardiac arrhythmias, and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Additionally, adherence to guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and the formal integration of a collaborative Endocarditis Team pathway (joint management involving cardiology, infectious disease, and cardiothoracic surgery) were evaluated to determine their direct prognostic association with in-hospital survival.

2.6. Statistical Analysis The distribution of continuous data was formally evaluated for normality using visual diagnostics (frequency histograms and normal Q–Q plots) and confirmed analytically using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), whereas non-normally distributed continuous variables were reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). Categorical variables were presented as absolute frequencies and percentages.

Inter-group differences in baseline characteristics, microbiological patterns, and echocardiographic findings between survivors and non-survivors were analyzed using the independent Student’s t -test or the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, depending on the cell distribution. Survival probabilities were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and survival distributions were compared using the log-rank test. Univariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with all-cause mortality during follow-up. Clinically relevant variables and those with a univariable p -value < 0.10 were considered for inclusion in a multivariable Cox regression model. Adjusted hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were reported. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using Schoenfeld residuals. To evaluate the impact of disease progression during follow-up, parameters demonstrating significant differences between survivors and non-survivors were incorporated into a composite clinical complications endpoint for both univariable and multivariable regression analyses. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided p -value < 0.05. Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 32.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and R (version 4.6.0; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

3. Results 3.1. Baseline Characteristics and Clinical Presentation A total of 470 consecutive adult patients diagnosed with infective endocarditis (IE) were evaluated across the participating tertiary academic centers. The mean age of the overall study population was 58.08 ± 16.81 years, with a male predominance (60.6%, n = 285). Regarding baseline comorbidities, hypertension was the most frequent condition (56.8%, n = 267), followed by diabetes mellitus (35.7%, n = 168), chronic kidney disease (34.5%, n = 162), and coronary artery disease (32.6%, n = 153). Furthermore, a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack was documented in 20.4% ( n = 96) of the cohort, while congestive heart failure was present in 26.4% ( n = 124) ( Table 1 ). When analyzing clinical presentation, fever was the most common symptom, observed in 61.5% ( n = 289) of patients, followed by dyspnea in 44.9% ( n = 211), myalgia in 26.2% ( n = 123), and arthralgia in 21.9% ( n = 103).

3.2. Acquisition Settings, Anatomical Distribution, and Predisposing Conditions Native valve endocarditis accounted for the majority of cases (65.7%, n = 309), whereas prosthetic valve endocarditis and cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED)-related endocarditis were identified in 24.5% ( n = 115) and 6.6% ( n = 31) of patients, respectively. In terms of acquisition setting, 58.9% ( n = 277) of infections were community-acquired, and 41.1% ( n = 193) were hospital-acquired. Anatomically, the mitral valve was the most frequently affected site (48.1%, n = 226), followed by the aortic valve (30.4%, n = 143) and the tricuspid valve (11.7%, n = 55). Prominent predisposing conditions and healthcare exposures included underlying valvular heart disease (50.6%, n = 238), recent hospitalization within the previous 6 months (45.2%, n = 212), prosthetic valves (26.0%, n = 122), central venous catheters (25.5%, n = 120), and chronic hemodialysis (24.5%, n = 115) ( Table 2 ).

3.3. Microbiological Profile Microbiological evaluation revealed Staphylococcus aureus as the most prevalent causative pathogen, identified in 27.9% ( n = 131) of patients, followed by Enterococcus spp. (13.4%, n = 63), coagulase-negative staphylococci (12.1%, n = 57), and Streptococcus spp. (7.9%, n = 37). Culture-negative infective endocarditis was recorded in 15.7% ( n = 74) of the cohort. Among staphylococcal isolates with available susceptibility testing, methicillin-resistant strains accounted for 45.3% ( n = 105) ( Table 3 ).

3.4. Clinical Presentation and Echocardiographic Findings At presentation, fever was the most common symptom, observed in 61.5% ( n = 289) of patients, followed by dyspnea in 44.9% ( n = 211), myalgia in 26.2% ( n = 123), and arthralgia in 21.9% ( n = 103). Echocardiographic evaluation demonstrated mobile vegetations in 59.6% ( n = 280) of patients and moderate-to-severe valvular regurgitation in 51.1% ( n = 240). Additional structural complications included paravalvular leaks in 20.0% ( n = 94), flail leaflets in 12.1% ( n = 57), prosthetic valve dehiscence in 8.1% ( n = 38), and paravalvular abscesses in 6.4% ( n = 30) ( Table 4 ). Empirical antimicrobial therapy was administered to 89.8% ( n = 422) of the study population, with vancomycin (45.7%, n = 215) and third-generation cephalosporins (36.9%, n = 173) serving as the most frequently prescribed initial agents. Among patients who received empirical antimicrobial therapy, treatment was classified as appropriate in 216 of 422 patients (51.2%), inappropriate in 170 (40.3%), and not assessable in 36 (8.5%) ( Table 4 ).

3.5. Clinical Complications, Treatment Modifications, and Outcomes During the index hospitalization, various systemic complications developed, most notably new-onset or worsening heart failure (27.9%, n = 131/470), septic embolism (25.1%, n = 118/470), sepsis (20.9%, n = 98/470), cerebral embolism (18.9%, n = 89/470), acute kidney injury (13.4%, n = 63/470), and cardiac arrhythmias (12.3%, n = 58/470). Support measures included endotracheal intubation in 16.8% ( n = 79) and total parenteral nutrition in 7.0% ( n = 33) of patients ( Table 5 ). Treatment regimens were subsequently modified based on culture results in 49.9% ( n = 224/449) of patients, due to inadequate clinical response in 15.9% ( n = 73/460), and due to adverse drug effects in 9.8% ( n = 45/459). Overall, a favorable clinical response by day 7 was achieved in 67.2% ( n = 311/463) of patients, and microbiological response was documented in 65.7% ( n = 290/396). Surgical treatment decisions were made for 40.6% ( n = 191) of the cohort, while outpatient management was selected for 25.3% ( n = 119). The 28-day mortality rate was 11.9% ( n = 56), and the mortality during follow-up was 26.4% ( n = 124) ( Table 5 ).

3.6. Comparative Analysis Between Survivors and Non-Survivors Comparative evaluations between survivors ( n = 346) and non-survivors ( n = 124) demonstrated several significant differences. The mean age was significantly higher among non-survivors than survivors (62.73 ± 17.17 vs. 56.42 ± 16.38 years, p < 0.001). Non-survivors had a higher prevalence of baseline heart failure (34.7% vs. 23.4%, p = 0.015), underlying valvular heart disease (60.5% vs. 47.1%, p = 0.011), and central venous catheter exposure (33.9% vs. 22.5%, p = 0.013). Furthermore, hospital-acquired acquisition settings were significantly more common among non-survivors compared to survivors (59.7% vs. 34.4%, p < 0.001) ( Table 6 ).

Mortality differed according to microbiological aetiology during follow-up ( p = 0.003), whereas the between-group difference in 28-day mortality did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.072). Candida spp. was associated with the highest observed mortality estimates, whereas culture-negative endocarditis showed comparatively lower estimates ( Figure 1 ).

Non-survivors more frequently presented with dyspnea (53.2% vs. 41.9%, p = 0.030). Echocardiographically, non-survivors exhibited a significantly higher frequency of mobile vegetations (76.6% vs. 53.5%, p < 0.001) and moderate-to-severe valvular regurgitation (64.5% vs. 46.2%, p < 0.001) ( Table 7 ). The non-survivors group had significantly longer post-endocarditis intensive care unit stays than survivors (12.0 [5.0–24.0] vs. 7.0 [3.0–13.0] days, p = 0.002). Post-discharge follow-up duration is presented descriptively and was not considered a prognostic variable ( Table 8 ).

Analysis of laboratory parameters revealed non-survivors had higher serum creatinine levels (1.60 [0.99–4.15] vs. 1.19 [0.83–2.89] mg/dL, p = 0.013) and CRP concentrations (109.0 [48.0–207.3] vs. 78.0 [14.0–153.0] mg/L, p = 0.001), together with lower eGFR values (41.0 [12.5–71.0] vs. 63.0 [22.0–91.0] mL/min/1.73 m 2 , p < 0.001). Non-survivors had significantly lower hemoglobin levels (10.02 ± 2.12 vs. 10.77 ± 2.43 g/dL, p = 0.002) and serum albumin (3.09 ± 0.87 vs. 3.32 ± 1.00 g/dL, p = 0.034), alongside higher white blood cell counts (13.24 ± 6.50 vs. 11.72 ± 5.63 x10 9 /L, p = 0.022) and systolic pulmonary artery pressures (38.34 ± 15.63 vs. 34.59 ± 13.57 mmHg, p = 0.025) ( Table 8 ).

Regarding empirical antimicrobial management, non-survivors presented a numerically higher rate of empirical antibiotic administration compared to survivors (94.4% vs. 88.2%, p = 0.050). While initial treatment modifications based on culture results were similar between groups, non-survivors required significantly more frequent regimen modifications due to a lack of clinical response (25.8% vs. 12.4%, p = 0.001). Consequently, non-survivors demonstrated markedly lower rates of favorable clinical response at day 7 (45.9% vs. 74.8%, p < 0.001) and microbiological clearance (52.9% vs. 66.1%, p = 0.010) ( Table 9 ).

Clinical complications were substantially more frequent among non-survivors, including sepsis (46.0% vs. 11.8%, p < 0.001), septic embolism (52.4% vs. 15.3%, p < 0.001), cerebral embolism (37.9% vs. 12.1%, p < 0.001), acute kidney injury (34.7% vs. 5.8%, p < 0.001), new-onset or worsening heart failure (37.9% vs. 24.3%, p = 0.004), arrhythmias (24.2% vs. 8.1%, p < 0.001), and myocardial infarction (12.1% vs. 3.2%, p < 0.001). Other complications, including spondylodiscitis, immune complex nephritis, splenic abscess, and pulmonary embolism, were also significantly more frequent among non-survivors (all p < 0.05) ( Table 9 ).

Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of mortality. In the univariable analysis, several variables including age (per 1-year increase: HR = 1.027, 95% CI: 1.011–1.043, p = 0.001), hospital-acquired infective endocarditis (HR = 2.101, 95% CI: 1.312–3.367, p = 0.002), mobile vegetation (HR = 2.005, 95% CI: 1.161–3.461, p = 0.013), eGFR (HR = 0.989, 95% CI: 0.983–0.995, p = 0.001), hemoglobin (HR = 0.842, 95% CI: 0.747–0.950, p = 0.005), systolic pulmonary artery pressure (HR = 1.019, 95% CI: 1.004–1.035, p = 0.015), ICU length of stay (HR = 1.019, 95% CI: 1.010–1.028, p < 0.001), fosfomycin use (HR = 9.161, 95% CI: 2.193–38.269, p = 0.002), treatment modification due to lack of response (HR = 2.593, 95% CI: 1.535–4.381, p = 0.001), clinical response at day 7 (HR = 0.397, 95% CI: 0.247–0.637, p < 0.001), microbiological response (HR = 0.529, 95% CI: 0.328–0.853, p = 0.009), clinical complications (HR = 6.649, 95% CI: 3.175–13.925, p < 0.001), and outpatient treatment (HR = 0.476, 95% CI: 0.297–0.762, p = 0.002) demonstrated significant associations with mortality, whereas the administration of any empirical antibiotic therapy showed no significant association (HR = 1.522, 95% CI: 0.659–3.514, p = 0.325) ( Table 10 ). However, in the multivariable Cox regression model, only hospital-acquired infective endocarditis (HR = 2.247, 95% CI: 1.216–4.167, p = 0.010) and the presence of clinical complications (HR = 4.207, 95% CI: 1.556–11.378, p = 0.005) emerged as independent predictors of mortality, whereas age showed a borderline association (HR = 1.021, 95% CI: 1.000–1.043, p = 0.053) ( Table 10 ).

To address the contributing components of the composite clinical complications endpoint and evaluate the distinct prognostic contribution of individual events, univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were performed for each specific complication ( Supplementary Table S1 ). While multiple individual events demonstrated significant prognostic value in univariable models, sepsis, acute kidney injury, cranial embolism, and myocardial infarction remained independent predictors in multivariable analyses.

During follow-up, 124 of 470 patients died, corresponding to an overall mortality rate of 26.4%. Patients with hospital-acquired infective endocarditis had significantly poorer overall survival than those with community-acquired infection (log-rank p < 0.001) ( Figure 2 ).

4. Discussion This large, multicenter, retrospective cohort study involving 470 adult patients evaluated contemporary clinical profiles, microbiological spectrum, management strategies, and predictors of mortality in IE following the publication of the 2023 ESC Guideline. Our findings provide critical real-world insights into the evolving spectrum of IE. In accordance with our study objectives, the primary findings are structured as follows: (1) evaluating empirical antimicrobial therapy in light of the changing bacterial spectrum revealed that Staphylococcus aureus (27.9%), with a high rate of methicillin resistance (38.9%), has consolidated its position as the predominant causative pathogen, driven by a major epidemiological shift toward hospital-acquired infections (41.1%); (2) assessing the precise prognostic impact of clinical complications demonstrated that in-hospital adverse events, particularly new-onset or worsening heart failure (27.9%), septic embolism (25.1%), and cerebral embolism (18.9%), are highly prevalent and critically dictate patient survival; and (3) identifying independent predictors of survival through multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis established that hospital-acquired IE (HR = 2.247; p = 0.010) alongside specific major clinical complications, notably sepsis (HR = 2.746; p = 0.001), acute kidney injury (HR = 2.479; p = 0.003), cranial embolism (HR = 1.971; p = 0.034), and myocardial infarction (HR = 2.200; p = 0.032), emerges as the strongest independent determinant of mortality in this contemporary nationwide cohort.

The epidemiological landscape of IE has evolved significantly over the past two decades. Historically dominated by oral streptococci and rheumatic heart disease, contemporary IE is increasingly driven by staphylococci and iatrogenic healthcare exposures [ 1 , 2 , 4 ]. Our cohort rigorously corroborates this paradigm shift. While hospital-acquired IE accounted for 41.1% of our cases, S. aureus was the most frequently identified pathogen (27.9%), with an alarming proportion of these isolates (38.9%) being methicillin-resistant (MRSA). Furthermore, the high prevalence of central venous catheters (25.5%), chronic hemodialysis (24.5%), and recent hospitalizations within the preceding six months (45.2%) underscores the mounting burden of medical interventions as predisposing substrates. These findings align closely with broader international data, such as the EURO-ENDO registry conducted in a multicenter setting between January 2016 and March 2018, which included 3116 adult patients diagnosed with IE according to the ESC 2015 diagnostic criteria. Infective endocarditis was identified as NVE in 1764 (56.6%) patients, PVIE in 939 (30.1%) patients, and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%) patients. Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients. The associated microorganisms were Staphylococcus in 1085 (44.1%) patients, oral streptococci in 304 (12.3%) patients, Enterococcus in 390 (15.8%) patients, and Streptococcus gallolyticus in 162 (6.6%) patients. Embolic events occurred in 20.6% of patients. According to ESC guidelines, 2160 (69.3%) patients indicated cardiac surgery, but only 1596 (73.9%) ultimately underwent it [ 10 ]. Despite significant advances in diagnostic imaging and surgical techniques, mortality associated with IE remains unacceptably high. In our cohort, 28-day mortality was 11.9%, rising to 26.4% during the follow-up period. In the EURO-ENDO registry, hospital death occurred in 532 (17.1%) patients [ 10 ]. Both our study’s findings and the EURO-ENDO registry highlight the urgent need for stringent infection control measures and targeted antimicrobial management in high-risk healthcare settings.

In our study, hospital-acquired infective endocarditis (IE) was significantly more prevalent among non-survivors compared to survivors (59.7% vs. 34.4%, p < 0.001). Similarly, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis confirmed that overall survival was markedly worse in patients with hospital-acquired IE than in those with community-acquired IE (log-rank p < 0.001). These findings indicate that hospital-acquired IE should not be regarded merely as an epidemiological classification, but rather as a high-risk clinical phenotype associated with adverse outcomes. Several underlying mechanisms contribute to this unfavorable prognosis, including exposure to central venous catheters and invasive devices, chronic hemodialysis, recent hospitalization, and a higher baseline burden of comorbidities [ 11 , 12 ]. Furthermore, healthcare-associated acquisition often increases the likelihood of resistant pathogens, leads to diagnostic delays, and complicates effective source control. Consequently, this vulnerable patient population requires prompt multidisciplinary evaluation and intensive clinical monitoring [ 11 , 12 ].

In patients with suspected IE, current guidelines recommend initiating empirical antimicrobial therapy as soon as possible after blood cultures are taken [ 1 , 5 , 8 ]. In our study, empirical antibiotics were initiated in the majority of patients (89.8%), with vancomycin (45.7%) and third-generation cephalosporins (36.9%) being the most frequently preferred agents. However, the fact that the appropriateness rate of empirical treatment remained at 51.2% and inappropriate empirical treatment was applied in 40.3% of cases indicates a significant need for optimizing empirical regimens in real-world clinical practice by considering the pathogen spectrum and local resistance patterns. Although traditional recommendations mandate emergency treatment in suspected cases, recent clinical evaluations question the rigidity of this approach in certain subgroups. A recent study investigating the clinical benefit of emergency treatment in hemodynamically stable IE patients did not include patients presenting with sepsis, intensive care unit admission, neutropenia, or a clearly identifiable focus other than IE. In 675 (55%) cases, empirical antimicrobial treatment was initiated immediately after blood culture, and in 555 (45%) cases, treatment was delayed until preliminary blood culture results were available. No significant difference was found between the groups in terms of 30-day mortality and the composite primary endpoint (5% vs. 5%, p = 0.894; 28% vs. 24%, p = 0.304, respectively) [ 13 ]. Although this valuable study in the literature predominantly focused on selected and hemodynamically stable profiles, our study successfully reflects the complex clinical spectrum of infective endocarditis owing to a large real-life cohort including high-risk patients requiring intensive care unit admission. As shown in the COSMO-IE study in Table 9 , neither initiating empirical antibiotics nor their initial appropriateness appeared to directly alter overall prognosis, a finding consistent with previous report [ 13 ]. Rather, our findings indicate that, while initial empirical choices were made, non-survivors exhibited a lack of clinical response, which subsequently led clinicians to attempt treatment modifications significantly more often. Therefore, the higher frequency of treatment modifications in the non-survivor group (25.8% vs. 12.4%, p = 0.001) and the lower rates of favorable clinical response at day 7 in this group reflect refractory clinical worsening and highlight the vital importance of adopting correct and targeted antimicrobial strategies promptly.

Echocardiographic findings in patients with infective endocarditis (IE) serve as the cornerstone of the diagnostic process and play a critical role in patients’ risk stratification and the determination of therapeutic strategies [ 14 , 15 ]. The size, morphology, and localization of vegetation detected via echocardiography are particularly decisive factors in terms of the risk of embolic events and hemodynamic deterioration. Furthermore, early echocardiographic detection of complications, such as valvular destruction, new-onset valvular regurgitation, or perivalvular abscess, is important for timely surgical indications [ 1 , 14 , 15 ]. In a study involving 779 patients with IE (66.4% male, mean age 65.0 years), symptomatic embolic events occurred in 234 (30%) patients. Multivariate analysis identified highly mobile vegetation as the strongest predictor of embolism risk ( p < 0.001) [ 16 ]. In our study, mobile vegetation (76.6% vs. 53.5%, p < 0.001) and moderate-to-severe valvular insufficiency (64.5% vs. 46.2%, p < 0.001) were found to be higher in the non-survivor group compared to the survivor group. However, in our multivariable regression models incorporating the composite clinical complications variable, which includes embolic episodes, mobile vegetation did not emerge as an independent predictor of mortality. As methodological considerations dictate, because mobile vegetation is a primary anatomical precursor of systemic and cerebral embolic events, the inclusion of embolic complications within our composite endpoint likely attenuated the independent prognostic variance attributable to vegetation mobility. Consequently, while echocardiographic parameters remain indispensable for assessing local tissue damage and acute embolic risk, their direct independent association with mortality in multivariable models can be statistically influenced by downstream complications.

Regarding the microbiological etiology, our results demonstrated that Candida spp. infections were associated with the highest mortality rates among all groups ( Figure 1 ). This observation is consistent with the aggressive clinical course typically documented in fungal endocarditis, which often involves extensive valve destruction and embolic complications [ 17 ]. Similarly, Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis in our cohort continued to present with a significantly poor prognosis compared to other bacterial pathogens. In contrast, the relatively lower mortality observed in culture-negative endocarditis cases, as highlighted in Figure 1 , may reflect a more indolent disease presentation or the successful initiation of empiric antibiotic therapy prior to microbiological diagnosis. These findings reinforce the necessity of early identification and aggressive management strategies for patients presenting with high-risk pathogens such as Candida spp. and S. aureus , as suggested in recent large-scale registries [ 10 , 14 ].

Multivariate Cox regression analysis revealed that the presence of significant clinical complications (new-onset or worsening heart failure, arrhythmia, sepsis, septic embolism, cerebral embolism, spondylodiscitis, glomerulonephritis, immune complex nephritis, acute kidney injury, splenic abscess, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction) independently increased the long-term mortality risk by more than four times (HR = 4.207, 95% CI: 1.556–11.378). This finding is in complete agreement with the literature, emphasizing that organ failures and additional complications play a central role in determining long-term prognosis in IE cases. In a large-scale national cohort study of endocarditis complications obtained using ICD codes, 38.2% of adult IE patients (mean age 60.3 ± 20.1 years, 48.5% female) developed one or more major complications. The most common major complications were cardiovascular complications (22.6%), neurological complications (16.7%), and renal complications (6.4%). Patients with complicated infective endocarditis had a higher risk of death (adjusted RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.11–1.13, p <0.001). Complications strongly associated with death were septic shock (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.27–1.30, p < 0.001), cardiogenic shock (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.20–1.29, p < 0.001), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) (RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.35–1.46, p < 0.001), and systemic thromboembolism (RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.05–1.08, p < 0.001) [ 17 ]. In this large-scale national cohort study conducted by Mir et al., it was reported that the risk of mortality increased exponentially in IE patients who developed complications, and the vast majority of observed deaths could be directly attributed to these complications [ 18 ].

A study on a prospective case series population was conducted to define the epidemiological, clinical, and microbial characteristics of critically ill patients admitted to the ICU with a definite diagnosis of IE, which included 325 patients (231 [71.08%] in the ward, 94 [28.92%] in the ICU). Following univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, the independent predictors of ICU admission were identified as vegetation diameter > 10 mm, abnormal PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and acute heart failure; furthermore, five independent mortality risk factors were identified: SOFA score > 14, absence of surgery, age > 70 years, acute heart failure, and embolic complications [ 19 ]. Similarly, in a single-center study conducted by Kazancıoğlu et al., it was emphasized that additional events leading to the worsening of the clinical status, such as heart failure and renal dysfunction, were among the strongest independent predictors of both in-hospital and long-term mortality [ 20 ]. The high risk ratio (HR = 4.207) obtained in our study confirms that systemic and cardiac complications occurring in the acute phase significantly threaten not only the short-term survival of patients but also their long-term post-discharge prognosis. In this context, early diagnosis of organ involvement and complications, along with the adoption of aggressive medical/surgical management strategies in the follow-up of IE patients, plays a key role in reducing mortality.

Several limitations of our study should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective, observational design inherently limits our analysis to previously recorded clinical variables. Second, while the COSMO-IE study successfully captures clinical and survival outcomes, detailed data regarding post-discharge functional status and quality of life were not systematically evaluated. Third, given the extensive spectrum of parameters evaluated in our multivariable regression models, analyzing each major complication separately in a single model was initially constrained by statistical overfitting and events-per-variable ratios. Consequently, our analysis utilized a composite clinical complications variable encompassing diverse events such as heart failure, sepsis, embolic episodes, acute kidney injury, and arrhythmias. Importantly, because these major complications developed during the clinical course rather than at baseline, this composite complication variable functions as an intermediate, time-dependent risk factor rather than a pure baseline predictor, which may inherently inflate hazard ratios due to conditional associations. Furthermore, due to limited event numbers within specific early sub-intervals, performing a formal 7-day landmark analysis or a separate 28-day mortality model was statistically unfeasible without compromising statistical power. Although we presented the univariable and multivariable associations of individual major complications to help readers interpret the driving components, the intermediate and time-dependent nature of these events must be considered when interpreting their prognostic impact. Fourth, despite the nationwide, multicenter design involving 27 centers across Turkey, potential center-level variations in diagnostic thresholds, antimicrobial protocols, surgical timing, and Endocarditis Team management may introduce institutional heterogeneity. Although performing a formal statistical adjustment for center-level grouping was precluded by the distribution of cases across participating sites, this real-world representation reflects routine clinical practice under diverse local resistance profiles. In this context, the rate of appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy observed in approximately half of our cases highlights a critical area for clinical improvement, while simultaneously enhancing the generalizability of our findings. Finally, patients with refractory cardiogenic shock or previous out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation were excluded to prevent extreme mortality confounding from masking primary risk factors, which naturally limits generalizability to catastrophic or terminal presentations.

5. Conclusions Contemporary infective endocarditis is a highly complex and fatal disease characterized by a prominent healthcare-associated burden and a predominant staphylococcal etiology. The occurrence of major clinical complications and hospital-acquired infections were the primary independent predictors of mortality. These findings emphasize that early identification of high-risk patients, rigorous monitoring for systemic complications, rapid microbiological diagnosis, and optimized therapeutic management, particularly targeting healthcare-associated infections and virulent pathogens, are essential to improving survival and clinical prognosis in infective endocarditis.

Background/Objectives: We aimed to evaluate the incremental diagnostic and clinical impact of extracardiac findings detected by [ 18 F]Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography ([ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT) in patients with suspected infective endocarditis (IE). Methods: This monocentric cohort study included adult patients with bacteremia and suspected IE who underwent [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT. IE diagnosis was based on the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria. Extracardiac findings detected by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT were assessed for their impact on IE diagnostic classification according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria and on clinical management. Results: Among 500 patients with bacteremia and suspected IE who underwent [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, IE was diagnosed in 211 (42%) episodes. Embolic events were detected in 60 (12%) episodes, with 42 (8%) episodes representing previously unrecognized findings. Two (0.9%) of the 211 IE episodes were reclassified from possible to definite IE according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID clinical criteria. [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT identified new infectious foci in 31 (6%) episodes (18 bone and joint infections and 13 vascular graft infections). Extracardiac findings on [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT resulted in prolongation of antibiotic treatment in 28 (6%) episodes and in a new indication for source control intervention in 23 (5%) episodes. Conclusions: Although [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT identified previously unrecognized embolic events in suspected IE, these findings had limited impact on IE diagnostic classification, supporting a selective rather than systematic use for embolic screening alone. However, its ability to detect occult extracardiac infectious foci may provide clinically relevant added value, particularly in patients with bacteremia of unknown source or vascular grafts. infective endocarditis embolic events [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT bone and joint infections bacteremia bloodstream infection vascular graft infection Duke criteria source control Staphylococcus aureus
