Introduction Embolic events are among the most frequent complications of infective endocarditis (IE), occurring in approximately 20–50% of patients, and are associated with a substantial impact on clinical outcomes [ 1 , 2 ]. In patients with bacteremia, particularly those at high risk for IE, the presence of embolic events raises suspicion of IE and typically prompts a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation [ 3 , 4 , 5 ]. Embolic phenomena are included as a minor vascular criterion in the Duke diagnostic criteria for IE [ 5 , 6 ], and are incorporated into several prediction scores designed to estimate the likelihood of IE among patients with Staphylococcus aureus or enterococcal bacteremia [ 7 , 8 , 9 ].

The central nervous system is the most frequent site of embolization, followed by abdominal organs [ 3 , 4 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ]. However, the majority of embolic events are clinically silent. Recent European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommend the use of [ 18 F]Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography ([ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT) not only in patients with suspected IE, in order to detect distant embolic lesions, mycotic aneurysms, and potential portals of entry [ 5 ]. Although [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, thoracoabdominal computed tomography angiography (CTA) and cerebral imaging are proposed for systematic screening of peripheral lesions even in asymptomatic patients [ 5 ], prior studies have reported a limited impact of cerebral or thoracoabdominal imaging, including [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, on improving the diagnostic classification of IE in asymptomatic patients with suspected IE [ 3 , 4 ].

Among patients with suspected IE, the contribution of cardiac [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT findings to diagnostic classification in the presence of prosthetic intracardiac material is well established [ 14 , 15 ]. In contrast, the diagnostic impact of extracardiac findings alone is scarce [ 16 ]. Therefore, the present study aimed to assess the usefulness of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT for the detection of peripheral embolic events in patients with suspected IE, and to evaluate the impact of extracardiac findings on IE diagnosis and clinical management.

2. Results 2.1. Study Population Among 3033 non-duplicate episodes with bacteremia and suspected IE in both cohorts, 500 episodes were associated with bacteremia and included a [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT examination ( Figure 1 ). The most frequently identified pathogen was S. aureus (215 episodes; 43%), followed by Enterococci (88; 18%) and Streptococci (80; 16%). ID consultation was provided in 496 (99.2%) episodes.

Transthoracic echocardiography was performed in 457 episodes (91%), transesophageal echocardiography in 316 (63%), and cardiac CTA in 36 (7%). IE was diagnosed by the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (ISCVID) criteria in 211 (42%) episodes. Among the 289 episodes in which IE was excluded, the most frequent alternative diagnosis was bone and joint infections (115; 23%), followed by catheter-related bacteremia (94; 19%) ( Table 1 ).

2.2. [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT The median time between the first positive blood culture and the [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT examination was 8 days (interquartile range; IQR: 5–11). Adequate suppression of physiological myocardial glucose uptake was achieved in 406 episodes (81%). Prior to [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, thoracoabdominal CT and spine MRI had been performed in 245 (49%) and 46 (9%) episodes, respectively. The site of infection was unknown prior to [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in 176 (35%) episodes. The [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT was performed to assess cardiac lesions in the presence of prosthetic cardiac material and to detect embolic events in 257 (51%) episodes, while in 243 (49%) episodes it was performed solely to detect embolic events or metastatic site of infection. Abnormal cardiac metabolic activity was detected in 106 (21%) episodes.

2.3. Embolic Events Detection Embolic events were identified by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in 60 (12%) episodes ( Table 1 ); 42 (8%) episodes represented previously unrecognized embolic events. Among the 255 episodes without prior thoracoabdominal CT, embolic events had been identified in 18 (7%). Among the 245 episodes with prior thoracoabdominal CT, embolic events had been identified in 22 (9%) by thoracoabdominal CT, all of which were confirmed by subsequent [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT ( Table 2 ). Furthermore, [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT provided an incremental diagnostic yield by identifying additional embolic events in 24 (10%) episodes.

2.4. Impact on Diagnostic Classification Among the 211 IE episodes, 56 (27%) fulfilled the minor vascular phenomena criterion according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria prior to the performance of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, with an additional 21 (10%) episodes meeting this criterion based on [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT findings. This led to reclassification of two (0.9%) episodes from possible to definite IE according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID clinical criteria ( Figure 2 A). When the 2015 Duke-ESC clinical criteria were applied, two (0.9%) episodes among the 211 IE cases were also reclassified from possible to definite IE ( Table S1 ).

2.5. New Infectious Foci and Impact on Clinical Management New infectious foci other than IE were identified by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in 31 (6%) episodes (18 bone and joint infections and 13 vascular graft infections). These findings resulted in prolongation of antibiotic treatment in 28 (6%) episodes and in a new indication for source control intervention in 23 (5%) episodes ( Table S2 ). Figure 2 B summarizes the impact of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT for the detection of previously unrecognized infectious foci and their impact on patient management. Among the 255 episodes without prior thoracoabdominal CT, [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT identified new infectious foci other than IE in 13 (5%) episodes (10 bone and joint infections and 3 vascular graft infections). These findings resulted in prolongation of antibiotic treatment in 12 (5%) episodes and in a new indication for source control intervention in 8 (3%) episodes.

3. Discussion In this large cohort of patients with bacteremia and suspected IE, the use of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT led to the detection of new embolic events in 8% of episodes, with no meaningful impact on the diagnosis of IE. However, in 6% of episodes, previously unrecognized findings led to changes in clinical management, including prolongation of antibiotic therapy or new indications for source control.

The proportion of embolic events detected in our study is substantially lower than that reported in previous studies, where extracardiac embolic or metastatic lesions were identified in approximately 46–71% of patients undergoing [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT for bacteremia at high risk for IE or other metastatic infection, and newly diagnosed foci in up to 10–48% [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. In our cohort, prior imaging findings were taken into account, and [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT showed at least comparable performance to conventional imaging (thoracoabdominal CTA or spine MRI) by detecting all previously identified lesions, while also identifying additional lesions. Several factors may explain the discrepancies between our findings and those reported in most studies. First, because [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT was performed at the discretion of the treating infectious diseases (ID) consultant or the Endocarditis Team, and mainly in diagnostically challenging cases, selection bias may have influenced the results. Second, prior imaging was not consistently reported in most studies, and it was often unclear whether lesions detected by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT were newly identified or already known at the time of the examination, despite a comparable delay between the first positive blood culture and [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in our study (median of 8 days) and in previous reports (median ranging from 7 to 11 days) [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. Third, most published studies focused exclusively on patients with complicated S. aureus bacteremia, who are at inherently higher risk of embolic complications or bone and joint infections than the broader population of patients with bacteremia of any etiology and suspected IE included in our cohort [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 21 , 23 , 24 ]. In the only study that took into account prior conventional imaging and included only patients with IE, a new embolic event was found in 29/152 patients (19%), which is comparable to that observed in the present study among patients with IE (16%) [ 16 ].

As expected, embolic events were more commonly detected among episodes with IE than among those without, an observation that is consistent with the pathophysiology of septic embolization from endocardial vegetations rather than from other, non-cardiac sources of bacteremia. Embolic events detected on [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT led to reclassification according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID clinical criteria in only 0.9% of IE episodes. These results raise an important question regarding the clinical value of systematic extracardiac screening for silent embolic lesions in patients with suspected IE, as currently recommended by the ESC guidelines, including in asymptomatic patients [ 5 ]. Although [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, like conventional thoracoabdominal CTA or spine MRI, reliably detects previously unrecognized embolic lesions, the detection of an asymptomatic embolic event rarely changed the diagnostic classification of IE and, on its own, infrequently altered management. This suggests that the diagnostic and therapeutic yield of systematic embolic screening may be more limited than previously assumed, and that detection of a silent embolic lesion does not necessarily translate into a meaningful change in patient outcome [ 5 ].

By contrast, the identification of occult, treatable metastatic infectious foci, particularly bone and joint infection and vascular graft infection, was the principal driver of management changes in our cohort. Prolongation of antibiotic therapy or the establishment of a new indication for source control occurred in fewer than 5% of episodes, compared with rates of 15–50% reported in prior studies [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 21 , 25 ]. Several factors likely explain this discrepancy. First, nearly all patients in our cohort were evaluated and followed by ID consultants, ensuring a thorough diagnostic workup, including microbiological assessment and conventional imaging, before [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT was performed, thereby reducing the incremental value of the scan. Notably, restricting the analysis to episodes without prior thoracoabdominal imaging yielded comparable results, suggesting that prior imaging alone does not fully account for the limited impact observed. Second, management changes reported in most prior studies were often driven by both cardiac and extracardiac findings, whereas our analysis intentionally focused on the impact of extracardiac lesions alone [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 23 ]. Douiyeb et al., who also specifically evaluated extracardiac lesions, reported that [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT led to a prolongation of antibiotic treatment in 8 (5%) of 152 patients, which is comparable to that observed in the present study among IE episodes (4%) [ 16 ]. In addition, a new indication for source control was reported in 18 of 152 patients (12%), a proportion higher than that observed among IE episodes in the present study (3%) [ 16 ]. This discrepancy may partly be explained by differences in patient selection. In the study by Douiyeb et al., patients transferred to other hospitals were excluded, which may have introduced selection bias, as patients remaining in the tertiary-care center were likely those with more severe or complex disease and therefore at higher probability of requiring source control interventions [ 16 ].

In the present study, all patients in whom [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT altered management had either bone and joint infections, mainly spondylodiscitis, or extracardiac prosthetic material, such as vascular grafts, consistent with previously shown [ 16 , 17 , 21 ]. These findings reinforce the notion that the clinical utility of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT is likely greatest in selected high-risk subgroups, namely bacteremia of unknown source or the presence of vascular prosthetic material, rather than in unselected patients evaluated for suspected IE. Ongoing randomized trials, including the [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT domain of the S. aureus Network Adaptive Platform (SNAP) trial, are expected to further clarify the clinical impact of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in patients with S. aureus bacteremia [ 26 ].

This study has several limitations. First, its monocentric, retrospective design over a 10-year period may limit generalizability, and changes in reporting practices, technology, and pre-imaging management over time may have influenced both [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT indications and interpretation. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, this remains the largest study to date evaluating the impact of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in patients with bacteremia and suspected IE, and consistent use of the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria throughout mitigates this concern. Second, the study is subject to substantial selection bias and confounding by indication, as [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT was performed at the discretion of the responsible ID consultant or Endocarditis Team rather than systematically, and was reserved mainly for diagnostically challenging episodes with uncertain IE or unclear infectious source. This enriches the cohort for higher pre-test probability of complex or atypical infection, and findings should be interpreted as applicable to this selected population. Only 500 of 3033 episodes (16%) with bacteremia and suspected IE underwent [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT ( Figure 1 ); among the 2533 who did not, 1474 (58%) were at low risk for IE and 609 already had a diagnosis established by other cardiac imaging [ 5 ]. Accordingly, our findings should be interpreted in the context of this real-world, clinically selected population and should not be directly extrapolated to an unselected population of patients with bacteremia. Nevertheless, the study reflects contemporary clinical practice and provides insight into the potential role of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT when used as part of the diagnostic work-up of diagnostically challenging bacteremic episodes. Third, use of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT also increased over time, particularly after the Endocarditis Team was established in 2018, which may have influenced patient selection and diagnostic yield [ 27 ]. Fourth, the incremental diagnostic impact of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT may have been attenuated because conventional imaging, including thoracoabdominal CTA or spine MRI, had already been performed in almost half of the episodes, limiting its incremental yield and direct comparison with these modalities. Fifth, although both cohorts have contributed to previous publications addressing distinct research questions, including the evaluation of IE prediction scores in patients with bacteremia, comparisons of different versions of the Duke criteria, the impact of cerebral and thoracoabdominal imaging on IE diagnosis, the incidence of embolic events in patients with IE, and the impact of the Endocarditis Team on IE outcomes, the present analysis is the first study from these cohorts to specifically evaluate the diagnostic and clinical impact of extracardiac [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT findings using the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria [ 3 , 4 , 7 , 13 , 24 , 27 , 28 ]. Lastly, since previous studies used earlier versions of the Duke criteria [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 28 ], a supplementary analysis using the 2015 Duke-ESC criteria yielded similar results, with only 0.9% of IE cases reclassified based on [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT-detected embolic events.

4. Materials and Methods 4.1. Study Design This retrospective study was conducted at Lausanne University Hospital, a Swiss tertiary-care center, and included patients enrolled between January 2015 and September 2025. Patients were drawn from the institutional cohort of patients with suspected IE (January 2015 to September 2025), in which all patients undergo both blood cultures and echocardiography as part of IE work-up, and from the bacteremia cohort (January 2015 to December 2024). The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Canton of Vaud (CER-VD 2017-02137, CER-VD 2021-02516).

4.2. Study Population We included adult patients (≥18 years) with bacteremia and suspicion of IE who underwent an [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT examination and had no documented objection to the reuse of their data. Duplicate episodes identified across the two cohorts were excluded. Suspicion of IE was defined by the concomitant performance of blood culture collection and echocardiography specifically to investigate IE.

4.3. Definitions Demographic, clinical, microbiological, and imaging data were manually extracted from electronic health records and verified by an ID specialist. IE diagnosis was established according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria and included episodes classified as definite or possible IE according to the final adjudication based on the complete set of clinical, pathological, and rejection criteria [ 6 ]. The presence of alternative infectious foci was determined by the ID consultant based on clinical, microbiological, radiological, and surgical findings. The decision to perform [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT, as well as its indication, either to assess cardiac metabolic activity in the presence of prosthetic intracardiac material, to detect embolic events and/or metastatic infectious foci, or to detect a primary focus of infection, was made by the responsible ID consultant or by the Endocarditis Team.

Embolic events detected exclusively by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT were defined as lesions not identified on clinical examination or imaging (thoracoabdominal CT and/or spine MRI) performed prior to the [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT study. Bacteremia was classified as community-acquired, healthcare-associated, or nosocomial according to the criteria proposed by Friedman et al. [ 29 ]. Sepsis and septic shock were defined in accordance with the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3) [ 30 ]. IE diagnosis was based on the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria, and included episodes classified as definite or possible IE according to the final adjudication based on the complete set of clinical, pathological, and rejection criteria [ 6 ]. Diagnosis of vascular graft infection was based on the Management of Aortic Graft Infection Collaboration (MAGIC) criteria [ 31 ]. Other foci of infection were identified by the responsible ID consultant.

4.4. [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT Protocol To suppress physiological myocardial [ 18 F]FDG uptake, patients underwent dietary preparation before the exam. This protocol evolved over the study period: initially, prolonged fasting for >24 h [ 32 ]; subsequently, a 72-h high-fat, high-protein, very-low-carbohydrate diet combined with intravenous unfractionated heparin (50 IU/kg, maximum 5000 IU) administered 15 min before [ 18 F]FDG administration [ 33 ]; or a shorter 24-h low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet combined with 12 h overnight fasting, administration of a high-fat low-carbohydrate beverage and intravenous unfractionated heparin (maximum 30 IU/kg) 4 h before [ 18 F]FDG administration [ 34 ]. Serum beta-hydroxybyturate was later introduced to assess the success of the dietary preparation in suppressing the physiologic [ 18 F]FDG myocardial uptake, using diagnostic threshold as proposed in the literature [ 35 ].

Two different PET/CT systems were used for the image acquisition, either a Discovery LS PET/CT (GE HealthCare, Waukesha, WI, USA) or SiPM 3D PET/CT (Biograph Vision 600, Siemens Medical Solutions, Knoxville, TN, USA). PET/CT acquisition was performed 60 min after intravenous administration of 3.5 MBq/kg or 2 MBq/kg of [ 18 F]FDG, respectively (depending on the type of scanner), followed by a low-dose CT for attenuation correction. Gated cardiac images were acquired over 10 min, followed by acquisition of whole-body images (from the skull to the feet). Images were reconstructed from the list-mode acquisition using time-of-flight and point-spread function information combined with ordered-subset expectation maximization iterative reconstruction into static images cardiac and whole-body static images. All studies were reviewed by experienced senior nuclear physicians. Adequacy of the suppression of physiological myocardial glucose uptake was assessed and paravalvular pathological uptake was assessed in patients with adequate physiologic myocardial suppression.

4.5. Outcomes The diagnostic impact of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT included the detection of new embolic events and new infectious foci, and reclassification according to the 2023 Duke-ISCVID clinical criteria [ 6 ]. To allow comparison with previous studies, a secondary analysis was performed using the 2015 Duke-ESC clinical criteria [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 28 , 36 ]. As the present study focused specifically on the contribution of extracardiac lesions detected by [18F]FDG-PET/CT, reclassification based on cardiac abnormal metabolic activity, an association already well established in patients with prosthetic intracardiac material [ 5 , 14 ], was not the focus of this analysis and was therefore not systematically re-adjudicated here. The impact of extracardiac findings identified by [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT on clinical management was categorized as either prolongation of antibiotic treatment duration or establishment of a new indication for source control intervention.

4.6. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Continuous variables were analyzed using the Mann–Whitney U test, and categorical variables using the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. No data were missing in the included variables. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and a p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

5. Conclusions In conclusion, although [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT can detect embolic events not identified by thoracoabdominal CTA in patients with suspected IE, these findings had limited impact on diagnostic classification, suggesting that systematic use of this modality, or of conventional imaging, solely to screen for peripheral embolic events for diagnostic purposes may not be warranted, and supporting a more selective approach. However, [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT also identified extracardiac infectious foci in a subset of patients, including asymptomatic bone and joint infections and vascular graft infections, with consequent changes in clinical management. Taken together, these findings suggest that the principal clinical value of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT in suspected IE lies in the detection of treatable occult infectious foci rather than in the systematic screening for silent embolic events, and that this modality may be particularly useful in patients with bacteremia of unknown source or with vascular grafts, in whom the likelihood of occult metastatic or graft-related infection is higher. Future randomized controlled trials are warranted to better define the incremental diagnostic value of [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT over conventional imaging modalities and to determine its impact on patient-centered outcomes.

Background Echocardiography is central to the diagnosis of infective endocarditis (IE). Although guidelines recommend repeating echocardiography when clinical suspicion persists despite negative or inconclusive findings, the diagnostic value of repeating transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) remains uncertain. The aim was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of repeat TTE in the diagnosis of IE among patients with suspected IE.

Methods This retrospective study conducted at Lausanne University Hospital (2015–2024) including adult patients with suspected IE who underwent 2 TTEs within 21 days. IE was classified according to the 2023 Duke‐ International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria.

Results A total of 503 episodes were included, of which 254 (50%) were diagnosed as IE. The second TTE was performed within 8 days from first TTE (interquartile range, 5–13 days). The second TTE identified new vegetations in 34 (7%) episodes and new paravalvular complications in 17 (3%) episodes. Sensitivity for detecting vegetations increased from 47% (95% CI, 39%–56%) for the first TTE to 57% (95% CI, 48%–65%) for the second. By excluding the results of cardiac imaging modalities other than TTE, the sensitivity of the second TTE for diagnosing IE was higher (45% [95% CI, 38%–51%]), compared with 34% (95% CI, 28%–41%) for the first TTE; the second TTE led to reclassification from possible to definite IE in 7 (1%) of cases.

Conclusions Repeat TTE modestly improved typical IE lesion detection; however, within a multimodality imaging strategy, its incremental diagnostic contribution was limited. These results suggest that repeated TTE alone is unlikely to substantially alter diagnosis in most patients, supporting the use of complementary imaging when suspicion of IE remains high. This study provides a comprehensive real‐world evaluation of the incremental diagnostic value of repeat transthoracic echocardiography within a contemporary multimodality imaging pathway for suspected infective endocarditis. Repeat transthoracic echocardiography modestly increased the detection of vegetations and other typical IE lesions but reclassified only 1% of episodes from possible to definite infective endocarditis according to the 2023 Duke‐International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases clinical criteria. What Are the Clinical Implications?

When clinical suspicion of infective endocarditis persists despite negative or inconclusive initial echocardiography, higher‐sensitivity imaging modalities, particularly transesophageal echocardiography and, when appropriate, cardiac computed tomography or [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography, should be prioritized over repeat transthoracic echocardiography, with imaging findings interpreted alongside clinical and microbiological data within a multidisciplinary endocarditis team. Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a major diagnostic challenge due to its heterogeneous clinical presentation and the variable sensitivity of available diagnostic tools. 1 , 2

Echocardiography plays a central role in the diagnostic workup, providing key imaging evidence to support the clinical diagnosis of IE. 1 , 2 Moreover, echocardiographic abnormalities constitute a major criterion in the Duke diagnostic frameworks, underscoring its pivotal role in confirming or excluding the diagnosis of IE. 1 , 3 Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is recommended as the first‐line imaging modality because it is noninvasive, widely available, and provides rapid assessment of cardiac structures. However, its sensitivity for detecting vegetations is limited, typically ranging between 40% and 63%, depending on vegetation size and patient characteristics. 4

Consequently, when TTE is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is recommended. Owing to its close proximity to cardiac structures and the use of higher‐frequency transducers, TEE provides superior spatial resolution and overall image quality, resulting in greater sensitivity for detecting vegetations or paravalvular complications. 1 , 2

Despite its diagnostic superiority, TEE can yield false‐negative results, particularly in early disease, when vegetations are small, or before the development of detectable perivalvular complications that may evolve over time. When TEE findings remain negative or inconclusive but clinical suspicion persists, complementary imaging modalities should be considered. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) is useful in both native and prosthetic valve IE, particularly for identifying perivalvular complications such as abscesses or pseudoaneurysms, for which it may outperform TEE. 1 , 2 , 5 , 6 , 7

In contrast, [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT ([ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT) is mainly recommended in suspected prosthetic valve or cardiac implantable electronic device‐related IE when echocardiographic findings are inconclusive. 1 , 2 , 5 , 8 An additional diagnostic approach in patients with persistently high clinical suspicion of IE despite negative initial imaging is repeat echocardiography. 1 , 2 The rationale for repeating echocardiography lies in the dynamic nature of IE: vegetations can increase in size and become detectable over time or new valvular or perivalvular complications such as leaflet perforation, abscesses, or fistulas may emerge. 9 , 10 , 11

Current guidelines differ regarding the recommended modality for repeat echocardiography when clinical suspicion remains high despite negative or inconclusive initial imaging. The American Heart Association advises repeating TEE after 7 to 10 days, whereas the European Society of Cardiology recommends repeating either TTE or TEE after 5 to 7 days. 1 , 2 This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance and clinical contribution of repeat TTE for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis within contemporary multimodality imaging pathways among patients with suspected IE.
METHODS The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

Study Design and Population This retrospective study was conducted at Lausanne University Hospital and covered the period from January 2015 to December 2024. Cases were identified from 2 institutional cohorts: (1) a cohort of patients with suspected IE spanning from January 2015 to December 2024, and (2) a cohort of patients with bacteremia or candidemia enrolled between January 2015 and December 2021. Suspected IE was defined as the combination of blood cultures being drawn and echocardiography performed specifically to investigate IE. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Canton of Vaud, Switzerland (CER‐VD 2021‐02516 and CER‐VD 2017‐02137). Owing to the retrospective nature of the study, the requirement for informed consent was waived by the Ethics Committee; however, patients who had previously refused the use of their data for research purposes were excluded.

Inclusion criteria were adult patients (≥18 years) with suspected IE; performance of a second TTE within 21 days of the initial TTE; and the absence of patient refusal of data use. Duplicate episodes identified across the 2 cohorts, as well as those in which the second TTE was performed after valve surgery or cardiac implantable electronic device extraction, were excluded.

Definitions and Classification We manually collected demographic, clinical, imaging, and microbiological information from patients' health records. Infectious diseases consultation was mandatory for all patients with suspected IE. Episodes were diagnosed as IE or no‐IE by the endocarditis team (from January 2018 to June 2024) or by expert clinicians (2015–2017; M.P.O., P.M.). 12 Episodes were further classified as rejected, possible, or definite IE using the 2023 Duke‐International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases clinical criteria. 3

We applied 3 sets of classifications: (1) using imaging findings from cardiac imaging studies performed before the second TTE, (2) including the results of the second TTE, and (3) reflecting the final classification after all cardiac imaging studies had been completed. In episodes with vegetation identified in both TTE, a significant increase or decrease of the vegetation size was considered if the change was >3 mm between 2 TTEs.

Echocardiography Protocol When a treating physician requests an echocardiographic examination, they must specify whether it is a standard study or one specifically aimed at investigating IE. In the latter case, the examination is performed or reviewed by senior cardiologists (G.T., P.M. with expertise in IE imaging. In our center, TTE image quality is classified by the performing cardiologist as poor, mediocre, adequate, or good/excellent. The designation of good/excellent quality is strictly reserved for examinations in which all cardiac structures can be assessed in detail and all myocardial segments are adequately visualized. For the purposes of this study, only examinations rated as good/excellent were considered of good quality. TTE was considered positive if it demonstrated the presence of a vegetation, abscess, leaflet perforation, prosthetic valve dehiscence, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, or fistula. TTE examinations were performed using Philips EPIQ systems with S5‐1 and X5‐1 transducers, Philips Affiniti systems with S5‐1 transducers, GE Vivid S70 systems with M5Sc‐D transducers, and GE Vivid E9 systems with M5Sc‐D transducers, according to routine clinical practice.

Statistical Analysis We used SPSS version 26.0 (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA) for the statistical analyses. After checking for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test, continuous variables were assessed by either Mann–Whitney U or Welch test as appropriate. Categorical variables were compared using the chi‐square or Fisher's exact test as appropriate. The diagnostic performance of the first and second TTE for detecting specific lesions, namely vegetation, abscess, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, leaflet perforation, and prosthetic valve dehiscence, was evaluated among episodes with suspected IE in which a reference standard (TEE, cardiac CT, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, valve surgery, or autopsy) was available. By excluding the results of cardiac imaging modalities other than TTE, the diagnostic performance of the first and second TTE for diagnosing IE was further evaluated by assessing the concordance between lesions detected on TTE and the final IE diagnosis according to the reference standard. We calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, positive and negative likelihood ratios, and accuracy with the corresponding 95% CI using exact binomial methods. Accuracy was defined as the proportion of correctly classified episodes among all evaluated episodes. Analyses were performed at the episode level and assumed independence between episodes, as recurrent episodes from the same patient were infrequent and represented distinct clinical evaluations separated in time. No data were missing in the included variables. All tests were 2 tailed, and P <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

RESULTS A total of 503 episodes in 486 patients were included from both cohorts, comprising 339 episodes from the cohort of suspected IE and 164 nonduplicate episodes from the cohort of bacteremia/candidemia (Figure 1 ). Seventeen episodes represented recurrent episodes in the same patient, with a median interval of 197 days between episodes (range, 63–2423 days). The first TTE was performed at a median of 2 days after blood culture collection (interquartile range, 1–4 days), and the second TTE at a median of 8 days after the first examination (interquartile range, 5–13 days). In 347 (69%) episodes, TTE was repeated due to persistent clinical suspicion of IE, as no typical IE lesions had been identified on prior imaging. In the remaining 156 (31%) episodes, in which typical IE lesions had already been detected by prior cardiac imaging, repeat TTE was performed for assessment of complications or follow‐up. Among the initial TTEs, 64 (13%) were considered of good quality, compared with 80 (16%) of the second TTEs. Overall, 284 (56%) episodes underwent TEE, 137 (27%) [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, and 37 (7%) cardiac CT. In addition, 94 (19%) episodes required valve surgery and 9 (2%) underwent autopsy. In total, 343 (68%) episodes had at least 1 reference investigation (TEE, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, cardiac CT, valve surgery, or autopsy); among them, 244 episodes had the second TTE within 10 days from the first. The timing of the second TTE relative to other cardiac imaging examinations (TEE, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, cardiac CT) is summarized in Table S1–S5 . Of the 503 episodes, 262 (52%) episodes had no other cardiac imaging modalities (TEE, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, cardiac CT) before the second TTE, and among these, 87 (33%) episodes underwent additional cardiac imaging after the second TTE.

IE was diagnosed by the endocarditis team or expert clinicians in 254 (50%) episodes, involving 161 (63%) native valves, 85 (33%) prosthetic valves, and 24 (9%) cardiac implantable electronic device leads. On the first TTE, vegetations were identified in 94 (19%) episodes, abscesses in 2 (0.4%), leaflet perforation or prosthetic valve dehiscence in 2 (0.4%), and significant new valvular regurgitation in 26 (5%) (Table 1 ). On the second TTE, vegetations were detected in 112 (22%) episodes, abscesses in 10 (2%), leaflet perforation or prosthetic valve dehiscence in 9 (2%), aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, or fistula in 4 (0.8%), and significant new valvular regurgitation in 48 (10%).

Compared with the first TTE, the second TTE newly identified 34 (7%) vegetations, 17 (3%) abscesses, leaflet perforations, prosthetic dehiscence, aneurysms, pseudoaneurysms, or fistulas, 27 (5%) cases of new significant valvular regurgitation, and 3 (0.6%) episodes with new typical lesions on a second valve (Figure 2 ). Table 2 presents the comparison between lesions detected by the first and second TTE and those identified by reference investigations (TEE, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, cardiac CT, valve surgery, or autopsy) among the 343 episodes with suspected IE in which at least 1 of these reference methods was available. The diagnostic performance of the first and second TTE for detecting individual lesions and for the overall diagnosis of IE is summarized in Table 3 . The sensitivity for detecting vegetations was 47% (95% CI, 39%–56%) for the first TTE and 57% (95% CI, 48%–65%) for the second TTE. The sensitivity for detecting other typical lesions (abscess, perforation, prosthetic valve dehiscence, aneurysm, pseudoaneurysm, or fistula) increased from 6% (95% CI, 1%–15%) with the first TTE to 22% (95% CI, 13%–34%) with the second. By excluding the results of cardiac imaging modalities other than TTE, the overall sensitivity for diagnosing IE increased from 34% (95% CI, 28%–41%) with the first TTE to 45% (95% CI, 38%–51%) with the second. Table S4 summarizes the diagnostic performance of the first and second TTE among the aforementioned 244 episodes. The results were consistent with the overall analysis, irrespective of the time interval between the first and second TTE. The diagnostic performance of the first and second TTE for the diagnosis of IE was also evaluated in the entire cohort of episodes with suspected IE, regardless of whether reference investigations were performed, and was comparable to the analysis restricted to episodes with at least one reference investigation (Table S5 ).

DISCUSSION In this study, the second TTE demonstrated better diagnostic performance than the first TTE for detecting typical IE lesions, particularly vegetations. However, within a multimodality imaging strategy, its overall diagnostic performance remained insufficient to safely exclude IE.

The second TTE identified new vegetations in 7% of episodes and new perivalvular complications in 3%. In comparison, previous studies evaluating repeat TEE have reported substantially higher detection rates. Shafiyi et al. found that a second TEE revealed new vegetations and new perivalvular complications in 36% and 8% of cases, respectively. 13 Similarly, Vieira et al. reported that repeat TTE identified new vegetations and abscesses in 14% and 2%, respectively, whereas repeat TEE detected new vegetations and abscesses in 47% and 35% of cases, respectively. 14

In our study, the additional diagnostic value of repeat echocardiography was modest, leading to reclassification from possible to definite IE in 1% of patients. This proportion is notably lower than that previously reported for repeat TTE (14%). 14 This difference is expected, as advanced imaging modalities such as [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT and cardiac CT were frequently performed in the present study but were not available at the time the study by Vieira et al. was conducted. 14

Both imaging modalities are now incorporated as major imaging criteria in the 2023 Duke‐International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases classification and have been shown to significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy for IE. 3 , 15 Previous studies evaluating repeat TEE demonstrated markedly higher diagnostic yield, with reclassification rates ranging from 17% to 47%. 13 , 14 This difference is expected, given the superior sensitivity of TEE for detecting both vegetations and perivalvular complications. 4 , 16

A meta‐analysis reported that, for the detection of vegetations, TTE had a sensitivity of 61% and specificity of 94%, missing many vegetations and most abscesses identified by TEE. The negative likelihood ratios improved when TTE was performed in patients with native valves (negative likelihood ratio=0.36) or when image quality was rated as good (negative likelihood ratio=0.17). 4 However, in the present study, only a minority of TTEs were considered of good quality, limiting its applicability in clinical practice.

The natural evolution of vegetation size during antimicrobial treatment remains incompletely understood. In the present study, vegetation size remained stable in 72% of cases, increased in 21%, and decreased in 7%. Furthermore, in 17% of episodes in which a vegetation was visualized on the first TTE, it was no longer detected on the second examination. These findings are consistent with previous studies. 9 , 10 , 11 Several investigations have reported that an increase in vegetation size during treatment is associated with a higher risk of embolic events. 10 , 11 , 17

Furthermore, an increase in vegetation size despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy is considered an indication for valve surgery, as it reflects ongoing or uncontrolled infection. 18 Although the second TTE in our study was performed after a median of 8 days from the initial examination, studies that repeated TTE at the completion of antimicrobial therapy have shown that vegetations often persist in the majority of patients (49%–75%) despite microbiological cure. 9 , 17 , 19

Importantly, the persistence of vegetation after completion of treatment has not been associated with an increased risk of relapse, suggesting that bacterial eradication occurs while the fibrin‐thrombotic scaffold remains. 19 Overall, these findings suggest that, within contemporary multimodality imaging pathways, repeat TTE contributes limited additional diagnostic value compared with higher‐sensitivity imaging modalities. These results question the European Society of Cardiology recommendation suggesting repetition of either TTE or TEE when clinical suspicion remains high despite negative or inconclusive initial imaging,

18 and instead support the American Heart Association recommendation to perform repeat TEE, rather than TTE. 2 However, these recommendations, originally introduced in the first versions of each guideline (American Heart Association 2005, European Society of Cardiology 2003), 20 , 21 predate the widespread adoption of advanced imaging modalities such as [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT and cardiac CT. In current clinical practice, imaging modalities provide complementary diagnostic information. TTE can detect large vegetations, particularly in native valve IE, but may miss small lesions or perivalvular complications. 1 , 2 , 4

TEE improves the detection of small vegetations and abscesses, whereas cardiac CT is particularly useful for assessing perivalvular extension. 1 , 2 , 5 , 6 , 7 In addition, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT can identify inflammatory activity, especially in prosthetic valve IE. 1 , 2 , 5 , 8 Particularly in patients with prosthetic valves and inconclusive or negative echocardiography, performing [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT and/or cardiac CT are often more informative than repeating echocardiography. 1 , 2 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 Nevertheless, repeat echocardiography remains a valid option when these modalities are unavailable or contraindicated. 1 , 2

Given the limited sensitivity of TTE compared with TEE, repeat TEE should be prioritized whenever feasible. 4 The present study has several limitations. First, this retrospective single center was performed in an institution with routine access to advanced imaging modalities, including [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, and cardiac CT. Consequently, our findings may have limited generalizability to other health care settings with different diagnostic resources. 22 , 23

Second, interoperator variability may have influenced echocardiographic findings. However, in our institution, echocardiograms performed to investigate IE are either conducted or reviewed by experienced cardiologists (G.T., P.M.) with specific expertise in IE imaging. Furthermore, since 2018, cases have been systematically reviewed during Endocarditis Team meetings, which likely minimized this effect. Third, the indication for repeating TTE, whether for diagnosis, assessment of complications, or follow‐up, was not systematically recorded in the data set. To provide context, we report the timing of the second TTE relative to other cardiac imaging modalities (TEE, [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT, cardiac CT) in Tables S1–S5 . Overall, 262 (51%) episodes had no other cardiac imaging modalities before the second TTE, and among these, 87 (33%) episodes underwent additional cardiac imaging after the second TTE. Nonetheless, in most cases, the decision to repeat TTE was made during multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team meetings. 12 Furthermore, because this study reflects real‐world multimodality imaging pathways, the incremental diagnostic value of repeat TTE cannot be fully isolated from the contribution of other imaging modalities. Fourth, selection bias cannot be excluded, as the study population likely included patients with less severe disease; patients who died early or underwent valve surgery soon after the initial evaluation were not included. However, such cases with life‐threatening complications would not typically undergo delayed reassessment with repeat echocardiography, thereby partially mitigating this bias. Fifth, the timing of the repeat TTE varied substantially across episodes. To minimize this potential source of bias, we performed a supplementary analysis restricted to episodes in which the second TTE was conducted within 10 days of the first. This analysis yielded similar findings (Tables S2 and S3 ). Sixth, the threshold of a >3 mm change in vegetation size to define a significant difference was arbitrary, though it was chosen to minimize the impact of interobserver variability. Finally, in the absence of an absolute reference standard, adjudication relied on endocarditis teams or expert clinicians with full access to clinical, microbiological, imaging, and surgical data. Although some degree of subjectivity is unavoidable, this process reflects best clinical practice and is consistent with current international guideline recommendations advocating for multidisciplinary case adjudication.

1 However, reliance on the Endocarditis Team's clinical diagnosis as the reference standard introduces potential misclassification bias. To mitigate this, we also applied the 2023 Duke‐International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for parallel validation.

Conclusions In conclusion, repeat TTE modestly improved the detection of typical IE lesions; however, within a multimodality imaging strategy, its incremental diagnostic contribution was limited with only a small proportion of cases being reclassified. Thus, when available, repeat TEE or advanced imaging modalities such as [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT or cardiac CT should be preferred when clinical suspicion persists despite negative or inconclusive initial echocardiography. Future studies should directly compare the diagnostic performance of repeat TTE and repeat TEE with that of [ 18 F]FDG‐PET/CT and cardiac CT in patients with initially negative or inconclusive echocardiographic findings.

Communiqué de presse 05/11/2026 Soins palliatifs pédiatriques : prendre soin de chaque enfant et accompagner ses proches

Les soins palliatifs pédiatriques regroupent les soins et accompagnements destinés aux enfants atteints d’une maladie menaçant ou limitant leur espérance de vie. Ces situations, dont l’issue peut être fatale, constituent une épreuve majeure pour l’enfant, ses parents, sa fratrie et l’ensemble de ses proches. En France, on estime à environ 100 000 le nombre d’enfants gravement malades et nécessitant le recours à une démarche palliative au cours de leur vie. Afin d’améliorer le parcours de soins palliatifs des enfants, adolescents et jeunes adultes pouvant être concernés, la Haute Autorité de santé (HAS) publie un guide parcours ainsi que des fiches pratiques. Ces travaux sont destinés à l’ensemble des professionnels intervenant auprès de ces enfants, depuis le diagnostic ou la reconnaissance de la gravité de la maladie ou du handicap jusqu’au soutien au deuil. La HAS entend ainsi favoriser une démarche palliative plus précoce et personnalisée, construite avec l’enfant et sa famille afin de préserver sa qualité de vie, sa dignité et son bien-être et, autant que possible, ses projets de vie. Ce guide propose des axes d’amélioration du parcours de ces enfants et les solutions envisagées.

The revised criteria keep the original format of the Duke criteria, including major imaging and major microbiology criteria, complemented with minor criteria [ 1–3 ]. Whereas methods for imaging have been revolutionized since the introduction of the Duke criteria in 1994 [ 2 ], the microbiological methods have developed but are still, in essence, the same. The more sophisticated imaging techniques have likely led to radically increased sensitivity and specificity as compared with the 1990s, whereas the sensitivity of the microbiological method remains high and the specificity remains low. This development should, in our opinion, result in a more pronounced emphasis on the imaging modalities in the diagnostic criteria for IE.

One of the changes in the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria is that Enterococcus faecium is no longer considered a “typical endocarditis pathogen” and thus 2 positive blood cultures with E. faecium are regarded as a minor criterion [ 1 , 3 ]. In the previous version, non-nosocomial E. faecium bacteremia with unknown focus was considered as a typical endocarditis pathogen [ 3 ]. It is generally accepted that IE is rare in bacteremia with E. faecium [ 4 , 5 ]. However, E. faecium can indeed cause IE and the consequence of the reclassification of the species is shown in Figure 1 with data from the Swedish Registry for Infective Endocarditis (SRIE) [ 6 ].

There were 7679 cases of patients treated for IE reported to the SRIE between 2008 and the present. Of these, 52 episodes (0.7%) were caused by E. faecium . Figure 1 demonstrates the consequences for the classification of these 52 cases by the proposed changes of the criteria. Importantly, in the 14 cases reclassified from definite IE to possible IE with the Duke-ISCVID criteria, 13 patients had vegetations demonstrated with echocardiography in conjunction with positive blood cultures with E. faecium . In 1 case, a patient with pacemaker vegetations was reclassified from possible to definite IE with the Duke-ISCVID criteria since pacemaker has been added as a minor criterion in the latter [ 1 ].

Figure 1. Consequence of the Dukes-ISCVID 2023 reclassification of E.faecium on IE , data from the Swedish Registry for Infective Endocarditis 2008–2023. Abbreviations: IE, infective endocarditis; ISCVID, International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases. The sensitivity of the ISCVID-Duke criteria thus decreases when E. faecium is excluded from the “typical endocarditis pathogens.” The Duke-ISCVID criteria chose to include nosocomially acquired Enterococcus faecalis bacteremia with known focus as a major criterion, although IE is known to be rare in this condition [ 7 ]. The argument for including E. faecalis was that the sensitivity of the criteria increased [ 8 ].

Our observations on E. faecium endocarditis point to the fact that it does not matter if a bacterium is a common or a rare cause of IE when the patient has IE as determined by echocardiography and concomitant bacteremia. We propose that the diagnostic criteria for IE could be revised so that patients fulfilling major imaging criteria and having significant bacteremia, irrespective of species, should be regarded as definite IE. In cases with negative imaging, the propensity of the bacterium to cause IE should be considered as well as other minor criteria. Notes Financial support.
